<doc title="Overview" path="guide/index.md">
# Overview

CoSky provides **configuration management** and **service discovery** for microservices. A small server sits in front of **Redis**, and applications talk only to that server. Redis is the one piece of infrastructure it needs.

## How it works

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph App["Each application"]
        STARTER["Starter or client"] --> VIEW["Local view"]
    end
    SERVER["CoSky server<br>+ Dashboard"]
    REDIS[("Redis")]
    STARTER -- "writes, leases: gRPC" --> SERVER
    SERVER -- "changes: Watch" --> VIEW
    SERVER --> REDIS
```

- **Writes** go through the server, which applies each one atomically and gives the namespace a new revision.
- **Reads** come from a view in each application's memory, so they cost no network round trip.
- **Changes** reach every view over a Watch stream. A client that was away resumes from the revision it last saw.
- **Everything is a resource**: a Config, an Instance, a Namespace, a Role. They share one API, over gRPC and REST.

[Architecture](./architecture.md) explains the data model and the consistency guarantees.

## Features

| Area | What you get |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Spring Boot `spring.config.import` with live refresh; YAML, JSON, properties and text; revisions with rollback; zip import and export |
| Service discovery | Spring Cloud `DiscoveryClient`, `ServiceRegistry` and LoadBalancer; instances under a lease; metadata and weights; fixed instances |
| Resilience | Local views keep serving through an outage; a snapshot on disk survives a restart; mass expiry protection; several server replicas |
| Security | ServiceAccount tokens and OIDC on every call, data plane included; roles scoped to namespaces and name prefixes; TLS; a structured audit log |
| Operations | One image with the Dashboard; Kustomize manifests; Prometheus metrics; OpenTelemetry traces; topology of who watches whom |

## When CoSky fits

- You already run Redis, and would rather not add a consensus system to your stack.
- A namespace holds up to about 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs, the size [measured](./performance.md).
- You want Spring Cloud integration, or Kotlin, or can generate a gRPC or REST client from its protos and OpenAPI document.

## When it does not

- Your data must survive any single failure without loss. Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the last writes. CoSky notices and recovers, as [Architecture](./architecture.md) describes, but it cannot bring them back. Use a Raft-based system instead.
- You need health checks run by the server. Instances stay alive by renewing a lease, and CoSky does not probe them.
- You need a client for another language off the shelf. Only Kotlin has one; other languages use the protos.

## Where to go next

| Goal | Page |
|---|---|
| Run it in five minutes | [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) |
| Serve Spring properties | [Configuration](./configuration.md) |
| Register and find services | [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md) |
| Use it without Spring | [Using the SDK](./sdk.md) |
| Run it in production | [Deployment](./deployment.md), [Security](./security.md), [Backup and Restore](./backup.md) |
| Find out what is wrong | [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md) |
| Move to a later 8.x release | [Upgrading](./upgrading.md) |
| Move from CoSky 6.x | [Moving from 6.x](./upgrade-8.md) |
| Look up a property or an endpoint | [Configuration Properties](./properties.md), [REST API](./rest-api.md) |
</doc>

<doc title="Getting Started" path="guide/getting-started.md">
# Getting Started

::: warning 8.0 is a release candidate
From `8.0.0-rc.1` to `8.0.0`, its API, wire format, configuration and Redis data only grow. It becomes `8.0.0` once it has run in a real environment for two weeks without a serious problem, so try it in one of yours before production. `ahoowang/cosky:latest` is still 6.x until `8.0.0`, when it moves to 8.0: a 6.x deployment should name its version, such as `6.2.0`. The documentation of 6.x is in the [`v6` branch](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/v6/wiki/guide).
:::

This takes a server in development mode and a Spring Boot 4 application. [Requirements](./requirements.md) lists the versions.

## 1. Start a server

```bash
docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 ahoowang/cosky:8.0.0-rc.3 --dev
```

`--dev` needs no Redis and no sign-in. Nothing survives a restart, so never run it for real: [Deployment](./deployment.md) shows how. Port 9090 serves applications over gRPC. Port 8080 serves the REST API and the Dashboard, at <http://localhost:8080>.

## 2. Add the starter

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.2.0"))
    implementation(platform("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-dependencies:2026.0.0"))
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-bom:8.0.0-rc.3"))
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webflux")
    implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-context") // for live refresh
}
```

In Kotlin, add the `kotlin("plugin.spring")` Gradle plugin as well: the bean in `@RefreshScope` below has to be open.

## 3. Configure the application

```yaml
# application.yaml
server:
  port: 8081 # 8080 is the CoSky server
spring:
  application:
    name: provider
  config:
    import: "optional:cosky:provider.yaml"
cosky:
  endpoints: localhost:9090
  namespace: default
```

The application registers itself as the service `provider` once its web server is up, and imports the Config `provider.yaml`. `optional:` lets it start while that Config does not exist yet.

## 4. Create a Config

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/default/configs/provider.yaml \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"config":{"format":"CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML","content":"example:\n  greeting: Bonjour"}}'
```

A bean in `@RefreshScope` sees the new value without a restart:

```kotlin
@RestController
@RefreshScope
class HelloController(@Value("\${example.greeting:Hello}") private val greeting: String) {
    @GetMapping("/hello/{name}", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE])
    fun hello(@PathVariable name: String): String = "$greeting, $name"
}
```

```bash
curl localhost:8081/hello/World
```

It answers `Bonjour, World`. Write the Config again with another greeting, and the next call answers with that one.

## 5. Find it from another application

A second application calls the provider by its service name. It takes the same dependencies, and `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer`:

```kotlin
implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer")
```

```yaml
# application.yaml
server:
  port: 8082
spring:
  application:
    name: consumer
cosky:
  endpoints: localhost:9090
  namespace: default
```

`@LoadBalanced` makes a `WebClient` take the host of a URL as a service name, and pick one of the instances CoSky knows:

```kotlin
@SpringBootApplication
class ConsumerApplication {
    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced
    fun webClientBuilder(): WebClient.Builder = WebClient.builder()
}

@RestController
class CallController(builder: WebClient.Builder) {
    private val provider = builder.baseUrl("http://provider").build()

    @GetMapping("/call/{name}", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE])
    suspend fun call(@PathVariable name: String): String =
        provider.get().uri("/hello/{name}", name).retrieve().awaitBody()
}
```

```bash
curl localhost:8082/call/World
```

It answers `Bonjour, World`, from the provider.

On a Mac with Apple silicon, Netty may log an error that it cannot load `MacOSDnsServerAddressStreamProvider`, as Reactor Netty brings the Intel build of that library only. The other one quiets it:

```kotlin
runtimeOnly("io.netty:netty-resolver-dns-native-macos::osx-aarch_64")
```

## 6. Look around

Open the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) at <http://localhost:8080>. Instances show up under **Service**, with **Leased** next to them, and the topology on the first page shows who calls whom. The server records the topology every 30 seconds ([`cosky.view.topology-flush-interval`](./properties.md)), so the consumer shows up there, and here, up to half a minute after it starts:

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/default/views/topology
```

## See it run

The repository holds this as a working example. `examples/README.md` walks through it:

```bash
./gradlew :server:run --args='--dev'
```

```bash
./gradlew :examples:provider:run
```

```bash
./gradlew :examples:consumer:run
```

## Next steps

- [Configuration](./configuration.md): formats, revisions, rollback and import.
- [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md): leases, weights and fixed instances.
- [Deployment](./deployment.md) and [Security](./security.md): before real traffic.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration" path="guide/configuration.md">
# Configuration

A **Config** is a named document in a namespace: a name, a format and its content, up to 1 MiB.

| Field | Rules |
|---|---|
| Name | Letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` and `/`, up to 253 characters. `shared/datasource.yaml` is one name. |
| Format | `YAML`, `JSON`, `PROPERTIES` or `TEXT`, declared with the Config. Only importing a zip file guesses it, from the file extension. |
| Content | UTF-8. The server keeps its SHA-256, which you can compare and cannot set. |

## Loading into Spring

```yaml
spring:
  config:
    import: "optional:cosky:order-service.yaml,cosky:shared/datasource.yaml"
cosky:
  endpoints: cosky.internal:9090
  token: ${COSKY_TOKEN}
  namespace: prod
```

- Only `default` exists at first. Create any other namespace before using it: `curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":{}}'`.
- `cosky:` without `optional:` fails the start when the Config cannot be loaded, including when no server can be reached and no snapshot holds it. When the server refuses, the start fails at once, and the log says why.
- YAML and JSON are parsed as YAML, and properties as properties. A TEXT Config becomes one property named after the Config.
- `cosky.config.load-timeout` (5 seconds) limits how long an import waits for the server.
- An import connects with what is known of `cosky.*` when its file is read, so keep these settings in the same file or in the environment. Spring reads `application.yaml` before `application-prod.yaml`, whose settings do not reach an import in the former.

## Live refresh

With `spring-cloud-context` on the classpath, a change to an imported Config publishes a Spring Cloud `RefreshEvent`, so beans in `@RefreshScope` and `@ConfigurationProperties` beans see it. This holds for a Config that did not exist at start as well. Turn it off with `cosky.config.refresh.enabled: false`.

The application compares against what it loaded, so a change made between loading and watching still counts.

When an `optional:` Config is deleted, its values leave the application on that refresh. A required one keeps its last values and logs a warning, because there is nothing to fall back on, and picks up again when the Config comes back. This also holds for an application starting from a [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) that the server no longer agrees with: it starts with what the snapshot holds, then follows the server once connected.

A Config that only another Config's `spring.config.import` names leaves the application on the first refresh that succeeds after that import is removed, unless another import still names it, and the application stops watching it. That holds for a refresh the application makes itself with `ContextRefresher.refresh()` as well.

## Writing

Use the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) or the [REST API](./rest-api.md). A write replaces the whole Config:

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/shared%2Fdatasource.yaml \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'If-Match: "42"' \
  -d '{"config":{"format":"CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML","content":"url: jdbc:mysql://db/orders"}}'
```

| Header | Means |
|---|---|
| `If-Match: "42"` | Only if it is still at revision 42. Otherwise `409`, and nothing changes. |
| `If-None-Match: *` | Only if it does not exist. |
| Neither | Write regardless. |

The Dashboard always sends the first two, so nobody overwrites a change they did not see. Writing the same content changes nothing: there is no new revision and no event, and the answer carries the revision the Config already has.

A `/` in a name is encoded as `%2F` in the path, because a name is one path segment.

## History and rollback

Each Config keeps its last 20 revisions, newest first:

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/app.yaml/history
```

Rolling back writes the content of an earlier revision as a new one, so the history only grows:

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/app.yaml:rollback \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"toRevision":"41"}'
```

A deleted Config keeps its history until it is created again or its namespace is deleted, and a rollback brings it back.

## Import and export

A zip file moves many Configs at once. Each entry path is a Config name, and its extension decides the format.

```bash
curl -o configs.zip localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs:export
```

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/staging/configs:import --data-binary @configs.zip
```

An import overwrites Configs of the same name, and holds at most 10,000 entries.

## Keeping secrets

Config content is not encrypted, on the server or in the [snapshots](./sdk.md#snapshots) clients keep on disk. Turn snapshots of Configs off with `cosky.snapshot.include-config: false`, and keep real secrets in a system made for them.
</doc>

<doc title="Service Discovery" path="guide/service-discovery.md">
# Service Discovery

An **Instance** is one running copy of a service: a service name, an endpoint, a weight and metadata. A service is simply the group of Instances that share a name.

## Registering

With the starter, an application registers once its web server is ready, and removes itself on shutdown. It leaves first, as soon as the application context starts closing and before the web server stops taking requests: consumers stop sending new ones, while a graceful shutdown (`server.shutdown: graceful`, Spring Boot's default) finishes those under way. Then the client closes and revokes its lease.

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
cosky:
  registry:
    enabled: true
    weight: 1
    metadata:
      zone: az1
```

- The service is `spring.application.name`, which must be a DNS-style name: lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `.`, up to 63 characters. `OrderService` is refused.
- A listener of Spring Cloud's `InstancePreRegisteredEvent` may add to the registration's metadata, as with Spring Cloud's other registries; what it adds is registered, and is registered again after a lost lease, while `cosky.registry.metadata` stays as configured.
- A separate management port is not registered.
- `spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled: false` turns registering off.

## Leases

A process holds one lease per namespace, however many instances it registers, and renews it every third of its TTL (30 seconds by default). When renewals stop, its instances go.

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| Clean shutdown | The lease is revoked within 3 seconds, and the instances go at once. |
| Crash | The lease expires, and the instances go a third of the TTL later: 40 seconds by default. |
| Lease lost, such as after a Redis failover | The client notices, waits up to 5 seconds so that not everyone returns at once, and registers everything again. |
| Client reconnects | It renews at once, without waiting for the next period. |

Allowed TTLs are 5 to 300 seconds.

## Finding services

`DiscoveryClient` and `ReactiveDiscoveryClient` read the local view. The first read of a service waits up to `cosky.discovery.load-timeout` (5 seconds), so that "not known yet" is not mistaken for "empty". If the server refuses, for lack of permission or because the namespace does not exist, the read throws a `CoSkyException` at once. Afterwards, a read costs no network round trip.

Add `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer`, and `@LoadBalanced` clients get their instances from CoSky, with Spring Cloud's own algorithms choosing among them.

## Weights

A weight of `0` keeps an instance registered but takes it out of rotation, which is how to drain one: load balancers leave it out, while `DiscoveryClient` still lists it. The Kotlin client's load balancer picks at random in proportion to weight. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer's default round robin treats every other weight alike.

An operator can set it on an instance an application registered. It lasts until the application registers again, after restarting or losing its lease, and so do metadata an operator changed: the application then registers what it was given. To keep an instance drained through those, set its own weight, `cosky.registry.weight: 0` with the starter.

## Fixed instances

An Instance without a lease stays until someone deletes it. Use this for something that cannot register itself, such as a database:

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/instances/orders-db \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"instance":{"service":"orders-db","endpoint":{"scheme":"tcp","host":"10.0.0.5","port":3306}}}'
```

The Dashboard marks each instance **Leased** or **Fixed**. Nothing checks whether a fixed instance is alive.

## Moving an instance to another service

An instance stays in the service it was created in. A write with another service is refused with `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (HTTP 400): delete the instance, then create it again. The default instance name holds the service, so this only comes up with a name of your own. An application registering under such a name for a new service is refused until the old registration is gone, which takes at most its lease's TTL if the old process did not stop cleanly.

## When things fail

CoSky favours keeping a stale instance over dropping a live one, and callers are expected to retry and use circuit breakers.

| Failure | What applications see |
|---|---|
| Server unreachable | Reads keep serving the last view, and the health indicator `cosky` stays `UP` with `connection: DEGRADED`, because a restart would not help. |
| Restart while the server is away | The view comes back from the [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) on disk. |
| Server or network was down for longer than the TTL | The reaper waits 30 seconds after recovering, so that live clients can renew rather than be removed. |
| A Redis Cluster shard fails while the others answer | Namespaces on the others are reaped as usual. Those on the failed shard are reaped 30 seconds after it last failed, once their clients could renew. Calls to a shard fail at once while the server's connection to it is down, and once the cluster has marked it as failed. A master that hangs with its connections open, its process stuck or its host gone, makes each call wait out the [command timeout](./properties.md#store) of 5 seconds until then, which takes the cluster's node timeout, 15 seconds by default: meanwhile reaping waits everywhere, as the reaper cannot tell it from the whole store hanging. |
| More than half of a namespace's leases expire at once | Reaping pauses, as this looks like a partition. It resumes when the share falls, or after 5 minutes regardless. |
| Redis fails over and loses recent writes | Every replica notices the revision going backwards, and clients start over from a fresh snapshot. Writes that were lost stay lost. |

These all have settings under [`cosky.lease`](./properties.md#server). A process that really crashed during such a pause stays listed for up to 5 minutes longer.

## Who calls whom

A client that watches a service counts as consuming it. The topology on the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) and at `/views/topology` shows these edges, under the name in `spring.application.name`, or the signed-in subject without one. They expire 90 seconds after the last replica saw the watch, so a stopped consumer disappears by itself.
</doc>

<doc title="Using the SDK" path="guide/sdk.md">
# Using the SDK

`cosky-client` is a coroutine client with no dependency on Spring or Redis. The starter is built on it. It needs JDK 21 or later.

```kotlin
implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-client:8.0.0-rc.3")
```

```kotlin
val client = CoSkyClient(
    CoSkyClientOptions(listOf("cosky-0.internal:9090", "cosky-1.internal:9090")) {
        token = System.getenv("COSKY_TOKEN")
        clientName = "order-service"
    },
)
val prod = client.namespace("prod")
```

`COSKY_TOKEN` is the application's own token: [Security](./security.md#a-token-for-an-application) shows how to make one. `tokenFile` reads it from a file instead, again once the file changes, so that a token rotated on disk needs no restart. Every setting but the endpoints goes in the block, and `CoSkyClientOptions.Builder` lists them with their defaults.

## Reading Configs

```kotlin
// Once, waiting for the first view.
val config: Resource? = prod.configs.load("order-service.yaml")

// Always current, from memory.
val current: StateFlow<Resource?> = prod.configs.watch("order-service.yaml")
current.collect { apply(it?.config?.content) }
```

`load` throws a `CoSkyException` when the server refuses the watch, such as for lack of permission or because the namespace does not exist, unless a snapshot knows better. The watch keeps trying, so a later `load` works once that changes.

## Finding instances

```kotlin
val instances: StateFlow<List<Resource>> = prod.instances.watch("payment")
val services: Set<String> = prod.instances.services()

val balancer = prod.loadBalancer("payment")
val chosen: Resource? = balancer.choose()
```

`choose()` picks at random in proportion to weight, allocates nothing and does not suspend. It returns `null` when no instance can be chosen.

## Registering

```kotlin
val registration = prod.instances.register(
    service = "order-service",
    endpoint = endpoint {
        scheme = "http"
        host = "10.0.0.7"
        port = 8080
    },
    metadata = mapOf("zone" to "az1"),
    weight = 2,
)
// ...
registration.close()
```

The client keeps the lease alive, and registers everything again if the lease is lost. Closing the last registration ends the lease.

Registering a name again replaces its registration, and the new handle is the one that closes it. Closing a handle again, or one whose name was registered again since, does nothing. A close that fails, as when no server answers, leaves the instance registered and renewed, and can be tried again.

## Errors

Reads, such as `load`, throw a `CoSkyException`, whose `reason` says why. `register` and `close` are writes, and throw gRPC's `StatusException` with the status the server answered, such as `UNAUTHENTICATED` without a valid token or `PERMISSION_DENIED` without a role that may register the service. Registering does not fail while no server answers: it goes out once one does. `CoSkyException.from(e)` gives the reason, as a `CoSkyException`, when the server sent one, and `null` otherwise:

```kotlin
try {
    prod.instances.register(service = "order-service", endpoint = endpoint)
} catch (e: StatusException) {
    if (CoSkyException.from(e)?.reason != ErrorReason.ERROR_REASON_PERMISSION_DENIED) throw e
    log.error("The token's account may not register order-service.")
}
```

## Closing

`client.close()` revokes its leases within 3 seconds. After that the server expires them.

## Connection states

`client.connectionState` is a `StateFlow`:

| State | Means |
|---|---|
| `CONNECTING` | No server has answered yet. |
| `SYNCED` | Following a server. |
| `DEGRADED` | Not connected: serving what is known, from memory or a snapshot. |
| `CLOSED` | Closed. |

Reconnecting backs off from 100 ms to 10 seconds with jitter, moving through the endpoints in turn. Each time it opens a new connection, to the next endpoint or, with a single one such as a Kubernetes Service, to that one again: a replica that cannot serve, being behind or cut off from Redis, ends the stream for the client to go elsewhere, and only a new connection can reach another replica.

## Snapshots

The client writes its views to `~/.cosky` (`snapshotDir`, or `cosky.snapshot.dir` with the starter) and starts from them after a restart, in `DEGRADED`, until it reaches a server. A `load` from a snapshot waits up to a second for the server to answer, so that a server that is there wins over a snapshot that is out of date, or from another server at the same address; where no server answers, it reads the snapshot at once. This helps a process restarting on the same disk. In Kubernetes it takes a persistent volume. Where the default directory cannot be written, as for a container user without a home, snapshots are off, which the client says once at info level.

Snapshots are not encrypted. The directory is `0700` and the files `0600`; a file system without POSIX permissions, as on Windows, gives them those of the directory they are in, which in the user's home are the user's own. `snapshotIncludeConfig = false` keeps Config contents off the disk, and `snapshotDir = null` turns snapshots off.

## TLS

```kotlin
CoSkyClientOptions(listOf("cosky.internal:9090")) {
    tls = true
    tlsTrustedCertificates = Path.of("/etc/cosky/ca.pem") // for a private CA
}
```

See [Security](./security.md#tls). For anything else, `channelFactory` builds the gRPC channel yourself.

## Writing

The client reads, registers and renews. To manage resources from code, use the generated gRPC stubs in `cosky-api`:

```kotlin
val resources = ResourceServiceGrpcKt.ResourceServiceCoroutineStub(channel)
resources.put(putRequest { resource = /* ... */ })
```

## Java

`cosky-client` exposes coroutines, which are awkward from Java. A Java facade is planned for 8.1. Until then, Java applications use the Spring Boot starter, which needs no Kotlin in your code.

## Other languages

Nothing in the client is privileged: everything goes through the public protocol. The protos are in `api/src/main/proto`, and `./gradlew :api:generateOpenApi` writes the OpenAPI document to `api/build/openapi/cosky.yaml`. A conforming client has to follow what the [design](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) says about Watch positions and lease renewal, and `conformance-test` holds the suite the Kotlin client passes.
</doc>

<doc title="Deployment" path="guide/deployment.md">
# Deployment

The server is one image, `ahoowang/cosky` (also `ghcr.io/ahoo-wang/cosky`), holding the Dashboard too. Run at least two replicas: they share nothing but Redis, and clients move between them by themselves.

| Port | Serves |
|---|---|
| `8080` | REST API, Dashboard, and Actuator unless it has [a port of its own](#actuator-on-its-own-port) |
| `9090` | gRPC, for applications |

## Redis

CoSky needs **Redis 7.0 or later, or Valkey 8**, with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. The server checks both at start and refuses to run otherwise, because an eviction would silently lose objects and Watch history. It works on a single node, Sentinel or a Cluster, and each namespace stays in one slot.

Everything that lasts is in Redis. Turn its AOF on, keep its data on a disk that outlives the container, and set `min-replicas-to-write 1` on a primary with replicas. [Backup and Restore](./backup.md) says why, how to back it up, and what happens when Redis loses writes or everything.

### Credentials and TLS

They go in `cosky.store.redis.uri`:

| Redis with | URI |
|---|---|
| A password | `redis://:password@redis:6379` |
| An ACL user | `redis://cosky:password@redis:6379` |
| TLS | `rediss://cosky:password@redis:6380` |
| Sentinel | `redis-sentinel://cosky:password@s1:26379,s2:26379,s3:26379#mymaster`. The credentials are those of the master and its replicas; Sentinels without a password were tried. |
| A Cluster | `redis://cosky:password@node:6379`, with `cosky.store.redis.cluster=true` |

Over TLS, the server checks Redis's certificate against the JVM's trusted authorities. For a private one, give the image a trust store: `JAVA_OPTS="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/tls/trust.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=..."`. A certificate the server does not trust stops it at start. `?verifyPeer=NONE` skips the check, for a test only.

`JAVA_OPTS` adds to the JVM flags the image comes with (heap at 75% of the container's memory, exit on out-of-memory, and what JDK 25 needs), rather than replacing them. The image is Eclipse Temurin's JRE 25 on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and runs as user and group 999.

An ACL user needs CoSky's keys and channel, which all begin with `cosky:`, and no dangerous command but `INFO`:

```
ACL SETUSER cosky on >password ~cosky:* &cosky:* +@all -@dangerous +info
```

It was tried on a single node with every kind of write, Watch and leases expiring, and on Sentinel and a Cluster through a failover. Without `+info`, the server cannot check the prerequisites above: it says so in its log, and starts.

## Docker

```bash
docker network create cosky
```

```bash
docker run -d --name redis --network cosky -v cosky-redis:/data redis:7.4 --appendonly yes
```

```bash
export COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
echo "$COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN"
```

```bash
docker run -d --name cosky --network cosky -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 \
  -e COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI=redis://redis:6379 \
  -e COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN \
  ahoowang/cosky:8.0.0-rc.3
```

Keep that token: it is the admin of a new installation, as [Security](./security.md#the-first-token) explains. Its secret takes at least 22 letters and digits, and the server refuses to start with a shorter one. For a Redis Cluster, add `-e COSKY_STORE_REDIS_CLUSTER=true`.

Any [property](./properties.md) can be set as an environment variable or an argument. `--dev` runs in memory without sign-in, for trying things out only.

## Actuator on its own port

Actuator's health, info and metrics need no token, and the metrics name your namespaces. On port 8080 they are open to anyone who reaches the API, so in production give them a port that only the probes and Prometheus reach. `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_PORT` (`management.server.port`) moves all of Actuator there. Port 8080 then answers 404 for `/actuator`, and the new port answers nothing but `/actuator`:

```bash
docker run -d --name cosky --network cosky -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 -p 127.0.0.1:8081:8081 \
  -e COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI=redis://redis:6379 \
  -e COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN \
  -e MANAGEMENT_SERVER_PORT=8081 \
  ahoowang/cosky:8.0.0-rc.3
```

- **Kubernetes:** `k8s/base` does this. It probes the port named `management` (8081) and leaves it out of the Service, so nothing that reaches the API through the Service, such as an Ingress, reaches Actuator. Prometheus scrapes the pods directly, by the `prometheus.io/*` annotations or with a PodMonitor on the port `management`, and needs no Service for it.
- **The image's health check** follows `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_PORT`. Set the port with that variable, or give the container a check of its own with `--health-cmd`.
- **The default stays 8080** in 8.0, so probes and scrapers already pointed there keep working until you move them.
- **The probes then ask the management server**, not port 8080 itself. To ask 8080 too, `management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true` serves liveness and readiness there, at `/livez` and `/readyz`, with the status alone.
- **With TLS,** Actuator's port speaks HTTPS too, unless you turn it off there: see [Security](./security.md#tls).

## Kubernetes

The repository holds [Kustomize](https://kustomize.io) manifests: a Deployment of three replicas, a Service and a PodDisruptionBudget.

```bash
kubectl create secret generic cosky-redis --from-literal=uri=redis://redis:6379
```

```bash
kubectl create secret generic cosky-auth --from-literal=bootstrap-token="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
```

```bash
kubectl apply -k k8s/base
```

For a Redis Cluster, apply `k8s/overlays/redis-cluster` instead. Your own overlay of a few lines can set the namespace, the image tag or the resources: that one shows the shape.

Each replica requests half a CPU, with no CPU limit, and 2 GiB of memory, which is also its memory limit, as [Sizing](#sizing) explains: change both memory values together. Replicas spread across nodes where they can, and the comments in the manifests say why each setting is there.

Probes use `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, on [Actuator's own port](#actuator-on-its-own-port). A replica reports ready once it has loaded the namespaces, which for 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs [took 2 to 3.5 seconds](./performance.md).

A replica stays ready while Redis is away, on purpose. Redis is shared, so a failover would otherwise take every replica out of the Service at once, while they can still serve what they know. The cost is that a replica cut off from Redis on its own goes on serving what it last knew. Replicas that disagree on `cosky_cache_revision{namespace}` for more than a minute show this, and restarting that one ends it. [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md#a-replica-cut-off-from-redis) has the other signs.

## Rolling updates

[Upgrading](./upgrading.md) says in what order to upgrade servers and applications. In Kubernetes a stopping replica first waits 5 seconds, for the Service to stop sending it connections. Then it ends its streams, after up to 5 seconds, and clients reconnect to another one and resume where they were. If they fell out of the Watch window meanwhile, they read a fresh snapshot, which costs a little more and loses nothing. `cosky_watch_gone_total` shows whether this happens, and `cosky.watch.window` is the setting to raise if it does, along with `cosky.watch.window-bytes` if your Configs are large.

Clients keep their connection, so after a rolling update or a scale-out the replicas that started last have few of them. Each replica ends a connection after about 30 minutes, give or take a tenth, and gives its streams 5 seconds, so clients spread out again: they reconnect through the Service, which is all the endpoint an application needs, and resume where they were. `spring.grpc.server.keepalive.connection.max-age` sets this, and `grace-period` under it the 5 seconds.

Draining a node stops its replica the same way. The PodDisruptionBudget lets one replica go at a time, so draining two nodes at once waits for the first replacement to be ready. On a k3s cluster of four nodes, draining each node in turn and then two at once failed no write, no read of a Config in an application and no registration.

## The Dashboard on its own

The image serves the Dashboard at `/`. To serve it under a path of its own, such as `https://example.com/cosky/`, or to host its files elsewhere, put it behind a reverse proxy that also forwards `v1/` under the same path to the server's `/v1`: the page expects the API next to it, on its own origin, and the server has no CORS. [Dashboard](./dashboard.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy) has what the proxy needs, with an nginx example.

## Observability

Metrics are at `/actuator/prometheus`. [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md) says what to do when one of them moves.

| Metric | Watch for |
|---|---|
| `cosky_cache_lag_seconds{namespace}` | Writes taking long to reach a replica |
| `cosky_cache_revision{namespace}` | Replicas that disagree for long: one of them is cut off from Redis |
| `cosky_store_apply_seconds` | Write latency, a histogram: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(cosky_store_apply_seconds_bucket[5m])))` is the p99 over every replica |
| `cosky_store_failures_total{operation}` | This replica failing to reach the store, by the store's operation, such as `tryLock` or `apply`. The replica stays ready meanwhile, and every replica's reaper asks the store for its lock each second, so one cut off from Redis counts even when idle: alert on `rate(cosky_store_failures_total[1m]) > 0` for a few minutes |
| `cosky_watch_active` | Watches on this replica |
| `cosky_watch_events_sent_total` | Events sent to watchers |
| `cosky_watch_gone_total{reason}` | Clients having to start over: `slow`, `compacted`, `epoch`, `regression` |
| `cosky_lease_active{namespace}`, `cosky_lease_expired_total{namespace}` | Registered processes and expiries. Only the reaper's leader reports them, so take `max by (namespace)` of the gauge over the replicas, which also covers a change of leader |
| `cosky_lease_protection_active{namespace}` | Reaping paused by a mass expiry, reported by the reaper's leader as well |
| `cosky_reaper_failures_total{namespace}` | The store failing on one namespace, such as one on a Redis Cluster shard that is down, while the reaper goes on with the others |
| `cosky_revision_regression_total` | Redis lost writes |
| `cosky_anti_entropy_drift_total{namespace}` | A replica's view differed from the store, which should never happen |
| `cosky_auth_failures_total{reason}` | Calls refused for their token: `missing` came without one, `invalid` with one that is malformed, unknown, revoked or expired, or an ID token the OIDC checks refuse, and `unavailable` could not be decided, while the access rules load or the identity provider is out of reach. Alert on `missing` and `invalid`, which point at a client; `unavailable` comes with an outage that other alerts catch |
| `cosky_auth_enabled` | `0`: authentication is off, and every caller is admin. The server also logs an error at start when it runs on Redis this way |

A namespace's series go when it is deleted.

**Traces** cover gRPC and HTTP at a 10% sample. To export them, set `management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint`, such as `http://collector:4318/v1/traces`.

**Audit**: every write and every authentication failure is one JSON line in the log. Collect those with the rest of your logs. See [Security](./security.md#audit).

## Sizing

[Performance](./performance.md) has the measurements. As a starting point, 512 MB of heap holds a namespace of 10,000 objects with room to spare, and memory grows by about 1.5 KB per object. The image sets `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` and compact object headers, so the heap is three quarters of the container's memory limit: give the container a third more than the heap should be, and request as much memory as the limit, as `k8s/base` does with 2 GiB for a heap of 1.5 GiB.

Large Configs need their own thought, because what is kept for resuming includes their content:

- **A replica** keeps at most `cosky.watch.window-bytes` (64 MB) of recent changes per namespace, on top of every object. Past that, a client that fell behind reads a fresh snapshot.
- **Redis** keeps the same in its log, plus the last 20 revisions of each Config and every object. Writing one 1 MB Config 800 times took 92 MB: 64 MB of log and 20 MB of history. At `maxmemory`, writes fail rather than anything being evicted.
</doc>

<doc title="Security" path="guide/security.md">
# Security

Every call goes through the server and is checked there, including what applications do. Nothing but the server touches Redis, so protect Redis and its credentials as you would the data itself.

## Who is calling

| Subject | Signs in with | For |
|---|---|---|
| `SERVICE_ACCOUNT` | A token, `cosky_<id>_<secret>` | Programs, and people without OIDC |
| `USER` and `GROUP` | An OIDC ID token | People |

A token goes in `Authorization: Bearer`, over gRPC and HTTP alike. The server keeps only its SHA-256, and shows the plaintext once, when creating it.

An account holds at most two tokens, which allows rotating without a gap: create the second, move the programs over, revoke the first. Revoking takes effect at once, including on open streams.

### The first token

On its first start, a server without any role binding turns `COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` into the `admin` ServiceAccount, with the `admin` role in every namespace. Use it to create real accounts, then revoke it.

```bash
export COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
```

- **Strong enough.** The secret, after the second `_`, takes at least 22 letters and digits, about 128 bits; the command above gives 32 hex digits. With auth on, the server checks the token at every start, used or not, and refuses to start with a shorter one or one of another shape, without printing it.
- **Read only while no role binding exists:** on the first start, and again when Redis loses everything, as [Backup and Restore](./backup.md#when-redis-loses-everything) explains. Otherwise another value does nothing.
- **After revoking it,** set the variable or Secret to a new token nobody has used, kept as a break-glass, or remove it. Left as it is, a Redis that loses its data makes the revoked token the admin again. Removed, nobody can sign in after such a loss until you set one and restart.
- Without it, a server with no role binding starts and logs a warning, and nobody can sign in.

### A lost admin token

A new bootstrap token does not help once anyone is bound, since the server no longer reads it. So keep a second way in, set up beforehand: an OIDC group bound to `admin`, or a second token of an admin account, kept offline. With it, create a token with `POST /v1/serviceaccounts/admin/tokens` and revoke the lost one with `DELETE /v1/serviceaccounts/admin/tokens/<id>`.

With no admin left, the last resort is a server with authentication off, on which every caller is admin:

1. Start one more server on the same Redis with `--cosky.auth.enabled=false`, where nobody else can reach it: outside the Service or load balancer, its ports bound to `localhost`. Leave the other replicas as they are.
2. It logs an error saying that authentication is off. Create a token with `POST /v1/serviceaccounts/admin/tokens`, and revoke the lost one.
3. Stop it at once.

### OIDC

```yaml
cosky:
  auth:
    oidc:
      issuer: https://idp.example.com/realms/main
      client-id: cosky-dashboard
```

The server checks signature, issuer, audience and expiry against the provider's keys. `sub` becomes the `USER` name, and the `groups` claim (see `groups-claim`) the `GROUP` names. The token's audience must be `audience`, or the client when that is not set.

The Dashboard signs in through the authorization code flow with PKCE, so register `cosky-dashboard` as a public client, with the Dashboard's address as its redirect URI and as the address to return to after signing out. The provider must allow that origin to call its token endpoint, and browsers and the server must reach the issuer at the same address. `GET /v1/auth/config` gives the page these public values before anyone has signed in, and holds nothing else.

`scopes` defaults to `openid` and `profile`. Add a scope only if your provider has it, because it refuses a request for one it does not know. Some providers ask for one to send groups, and some for `offline_access` to give a refresh token.

- **Staying signed in.** The Dashboard renews the ID token before it expires, using the refresh token. A provider that gives none leaves people to sign in again when the token expires, which takes 5 minutes on a default Keycloak. The refresh token stays in the tab, next to the ID token, and ends with it. A live view ends when the ID token it was opened with expires, and the Dashboard opens it again with the renewed one: someone removed from a group at the provider stops seeing what the group may within one token's lifetime.
- **Signing out** also ends the session at the provider, so that the next sign-in asks for a password, if the provider has an `end_session_endpoint`.
- **When the provider is away,** servers still start, and applications carry on with their tokens. People already signed in carry on until their ID token expires, and new sign-ins fail: the server answers `UNAVAILABLE` (`IDENTITY_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE`) rather than calling the token invalid. Keep a ServiceAccount token to get in meanwhile.

### Keycloak

This was tried with Keycloak 26. Other providers follow the same standard, but none has been tried.

1. Create the client `cosky-dashboard`, with client authentication off and the standard flow on. Set its valid redirect URIs to `https://cosky.example.com/*` and its web origins to `https://cosky.example.com`.
2. In the client's dedicated scope, add a **Group Membership** mapper with the token claim name `groups`, **Full group path** off, and **Add to ID token** on. With the full path on, a group's name is `/devs`.
3. Bind a role to the group. A person's `sub` is an opaque id, so groups are easier. Someone with no role yet sees their `sub` and groups in the Dashboard, to pass on to you.

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/rolebindings/devs-view \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"roleBinding":{"role":"viewer","subjects":[{"type":"TYPE_GROUP","name":"devs"}],"namespaces":["*"]}}'
```

## Who may do what

A **Role** holds rules, and a **RoleBinding** gives a role to subjects in some namespaces. Four roles are built in, and a Role cannot take their names:

| Role | Allows |
|---|---|
| `admin` | Everything |
| `viewer` | Reading and watching everything |
| `client` | Reading and watching Configs, and reading, watching and writing Instances |
| `service` | As `client`, but writing only the Instances of the service named like the subject |

### A token for an application

Every namespace comes with a ServiceAccount of its own name, bound to `client` there. The applications of a namespace share its token and need nothing else. Create the token once, in the Dashboard under **Security** with **Create token** on the account named like the namespace, or with an admin's token in `COSKY_TOKEN`:

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/serviceaccounts/prod/tokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

It answers the token, once. Give it to the applications as `cosky.token` (`COSKY_TOKEN`). An application without a token, or with one its roles do not allow, stops at start and says which.

- **For this namespace only, and this one only.** Deleted and created again, a namespace is new, and so is its account, without tokens: the old token reaches nothing.
- **Yours stays yours.** A ServiceAccount or RoleBinding of that name you made yourself is left alone, and that namespace then has no account of its own.
- **Off:** `cosky.auth.namespace-accounts: false`. The accounts made already stay until you delete them.

To tell applications apart, to revoke one alone or to see in the audit log who did what, give an application a ServiceAccount named like its service, bound to `service`: it registers that service and no other, and reads like `client`.

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/serviceaccounts/order \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"serviceAccount":{"description":"The order service"}}'
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/rolebindings/order-service \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"roleBinding":{"role":"service","subjects":[{"type":"TYPE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT","name":"order"}],"namespaces":["prod"]}}'
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/serviceaccounts/order/tokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

For less still, such as reading its own Configs only, write a role of your own.

Your own roles look like this:

```json
{
  "role": {
    "description": "Runs the order service",
    "rules": [
      {"kinds": ["KIND_INSTANCE"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_PUT", "VERB_DELETE"], "names": ["order"]},
      {"kinds": ["KIND_INSTANCE"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_GET", "VERB_WATCH"]},
      {"kinds": ["KIND_CONFIG"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_GET", "VERB_WATCH"], "names": ["order-service.yaml", "shared/*"]}
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "roleBinding": {
    "role": "order-service",
    "subjects": [{"type": "TYPE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT", "name": "order"}],
    "namespaces": ["prod"]
  }
}
```

- A call is allowed when any rule of any bound role matches it. A rule applies only where its own namespaces and the binding's overlap.
- `names` left empty matches everything. Otherwise it holds exact values, or prefixes ending in `*`, matched against the Config name, the Instance's **service**, or the object name.
- Global kinds (Namespace, ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding) live in the namespace `_system`.
- Nobody gives more than they hold. Writing a Role takes holding each of its rules in every namespace the rule names, `*` only by holding it in `*`. Writing a RoleBinding takes holding what its role grants in the binding's namespaces: for `service`, the Instances of each subject's own service, or of any service for a group, and for a role that does not exist yet, everything there. Creating a token for a ServiceAccount takes holding everything that account may do. Otherwise the server answers `PERMISSION_DENIED`, saying what you do not hold. An admin holds everything, so this never stops one.
- Writing Roles, RoleBindings and ServiceAccounts still lets someone take access away from others, and give anyone what they hold themselves: grant it to those who manage access.
- `GET` includes lists, and only what the rule allows shows up in them.
- A lease belongs to whoever took it, so one account cannot attach its instances to another's lease.
- A change to a role reaches open Watch streams: one that lost permission is canceled.

`GET /v1/me` shows who the server thinks you are, and your effective rules.

With `cosky.auth.enabled: false` everyone may do everything. It is for development only: on Redis, the server logs an error at every start, and reports `cosky_auth_enabled 0` (see [Deployment](./deployment.md#observability)).

## TLS

Without TLS, tokens cross the network in the clear, so turn it on in production. The server uses Spring's SSL bundles:

```yaml
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      jks:
        cosky:
          keystore:
            location: file:/etc/cosky/server.p12
            password: ${KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
            type: PKCS12
  grpc:
    server:
      ssl:
        bundle: cosky
server:
  ssl:
    bundle: cosky
```

And clients:

```yaml
cosky:
  tls:
    enabled: true
    trusted-certificates: /etc/cosky/ca.pem   # for a private CA; otherwise the JVM's trust store decides
```

Mutual TLS is not supported yet: a client proves who it is with its token.

With TLS on, port 8080 speaks only HTTPS, and so does [Actuator's own port](./deployment.md#actuator-on-its-own-port), which takes the same settings, while the image's health check and the probes in `k8s/base` use HTTP. Keep Actuator's port plain:

```yaml
management:
  server:
    port: 8081
    ssl:
      enabled: false
```

`k8s/base` already probes port 8081: add `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_SSL_ENABLED=false` to its environment. The image's health check follows `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_PORT`, so set the port that way, or give the container a check of its own: `docker run --health-cmd 'curl -f http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/liveness || exit 1'`.

## Audit

Each write and each failed sign-in is one JSON line in the log, with the time, subject, verb, kind, namespace, name, revision, outcome and remote address. Config contents and tokens never appear. The server keeps no audit data of its own: collect the lines with your log system, which also decides how long they stay.

## What is not protected

- Config contents are not encrypted, in Redis or in client [snapshots](./sdk.md#snapshots).
- Anyone who can reach Redis can read and change everything, past all of the above. Give the server a Redis user of its own, over TLS where others share the network: see [Deployment](./deployment.md#credentials-and-tls).
- Instance metadata is visible to anyone allowed to read the instance.
- The REST API's document, `/v3/api-docs`, and Swagger UI, `/swagger-ui.html`, need no token; calls made from it do. `springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false` turns both off.
- `/actuator/health`, `/actuator/info` and `/actuator/prometheus` need no token, and the metrics name your namespaces. They are on port 8080 unless moved: give them [a port of their own](./deployment.md#actuator-on-its-own-port) that only the probes and Prometheus reach, as `k8s/base` does.
- gRPC health on port 9090 needs no token. gRPC reflection is off, and `spring.grpc.server.reflection.enabled` turns it on.
</doc>

<doc title="Dashboard" path="guide/dashboard.md">
# Dashboard

The server hosts the Dashboard at `/`, on port 8080, and a reverse proxy can serve it under a path of its own ([Behind a reverse proxy](#behind-a-reverse-proxy)). It uses only the public [REST API](./rest-api.md), so it can do nothing you could not do with `curl`, and your [roles](./security.md#who-may-do-what) apply to it. A refused action shows the server's reason.

![Dashboard](/dashboard-dashboard.png)

## Signing in

Paste a ServiceAccount token, or use the OIDC button when the server [offers one](./security.md#oidc). The token stays in that browser tab, and goes when the tab closes. A server with `cosky.auth.enabled: false` asks for nothing.

## Pages

The namespace selector in the header decides what every page shows.

| Page | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Dashboard** | Counts of services, instances, Configs and namespaces, and the topology of who watches whom |
| **Configuration** | Create, edit, delete, import and export Configs; compare any revision with the current one, and roll back |
| **Service** | Services and their instances, leased or fixed; add, edit and delete instances |
| **Namespace** | Create and delete namespaces. Only an empty one can be deleted, and not the one selected. |
| **Service Account** | Accounts and their tokens. A new token shows once, so copy it then. |
| **Role** and **Role Binding** | Who may do what, and where |

A list shows 10 rows a page. **Rows per page**, under the list, shows 20, 50 or 100 instead, and the browser remembers the choice for each list. A search covers every page.

![Configuration](/dashboard-config.png)

## Staying current

The Configuration and Service pages follow changes as they happen, over a server-sent event stream, without a reload. A stream that breaks or goes silent is opened again. The first page reads its counts every 30 seconds, so that it does not hold a connection of its own: browsers allow few per server over HTTP/1.1.

## Editing safely

An edit remembers the revision it started from. If someone changed the object in the meantime, saving fails with the server's reason and changes nothing, so reload and try again.

## Behind a reverse proxy

The same Dashboard works at the root and under any path, such as `https://example.com/cosky/`, without being built again. It loads its files and calls the API relative to its own address, and keeps its routes in the fragment (`#/config`), so a reload or a link to one of its pages only ever asks for that address. Signing in with [OIDC](./security.md#oidc) returns to it as well: register `https://example.com/cosky/` with the provider.

A proxy that serves the Dashboard under a path has to:

- **Pass on everything under the path, without it**: `/cosky/` reaches the server's `/`, `/cosky/assets/...` its `/assets/...`, and `/cosky/v1/...` the REST API at `/v1/...`.
- **Redirect the path without its trailing slash**, `/cosky`, to `/cosky/`. Without the slash, the browser resolves the page's addresses against `/`.
- **Not buffer responses**, so that the changes of [Staying current](#staying-current) arrive when they are sent. An idle stream carries a bookmark every [`cosky.watch.progress-interval`](./properties.md) (10 seconds), so any read timeout longer than that holds.

With nginx:

```nginx
location /cosky/ {
    # The trailing slash of the URI replaces /cosky/ with /, and has nginx redirect /cosky to /cosky/.
    proxy_pass http://cosky-server:8080/;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    # Server-sent events: pass each one on as it comes.
    proxy_buffering off;
}
```

To serve the files of `dashboard/dist` from somewhere else instead, serve them at the path, and pass on only `/cosky/v1/` to the server's `/v1/`, unbuffered: the page expects the API next to it, on its own origin, since the server has no CORS.
</doc>

<doc title="Backup and Restore" path="guide/backup.md">
# Backup and Restore

This page is for operators. The server keeps nothing on disk: everything that lasts is in Redis. Here is what is there, how to make Redis keep it, and how to get it back.

## What is in Redis

All of CoSky's keys begin with `cosky:`, and each namespace's keys share the hash tag `cosky:{<namespace>}:`, so that a namespace stays in one slot. The design document has [the layout](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md).

| What | Notes |
|---|---|
| Every object, with its revision, its times and who last changed it | Configs and Instances in their namespace. Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, Roles and RoleBindings in `_system`. |
| The last 20 revisions of each Config | Its history, for rollback |
| Each namespace's change log | Up to `cosky.watch.window` entries and `cosky.watch.window-bytes`. Clients resume from it. |
| Each namespace's revision and epoch | What a client's position means, as [Architecture](./architecture.md#when-redis-loses-writes) explains |
| Leases, with their expiry, TTL and owner | The instances attached to one go when it expires |
| The topology | Written again by every replica every 30 seconds |
| The reaper's lock | Held for seconds |

Tokens are kept as their SHA-256 only, so a backup holds none that could be used. It does hold Config contents as they are, unencrypted: protect backups as you protect Redis.

Three things are not in Redis: the [audit log](./security.md#audit), which is in the server's log; the bootstrap token, which is in your environment or Secret; and the clients' [snapshots](./sdk.md#snapshots), on their own disks.

## What Redis must do

- **`maxmemory-policy noeviction`.** The server refuses to start without it, as [Deployment](./deployment.md#redis) says.
- **AOF: `appendonly yes`.** Its default `appendfsync everysec` loses at most about the last second of writes when Redis crashes. Without AOF, a restart takes Redis back to its last RDB snapshot, which with the default save points can be an hour old, and loses everything written since.
- **A disk that outlives the container**, for Redis's data directory.
- **`min-replicas-to-write 1`**, with `min-replicas-max-lag 10`, on a primary with replicas. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the writes that had not reached the replica. These narrow that window. The cost is that the primary refuses writes while no replica is connected and caught up: CoSky then answers `STORE_UNAVAILABLE`, while reads and running applications go on.

Redis starts with `noeviction` by default. In Docker, a volume and one flag give the rest:

```bash
docker run -d --name redis --network cosky -v cosky-redis:/data redis:7.4 --appendonly yes
```

A managed Redis has these as settings of its own. Check that persistence is on and that the eviction policy is `noeviction`.

## When Redis loses data

### When a failover loses the last writes

A Config written just before a failover may be gone, and so may a token revocation or a change of a role. CoSky notices that the revision went back: `cosky_revision_regression_total` rises, and a replica logs an error that names the namespace and the revision it went back to. Every replica then loads the namespace again, every client starts over from what Redis has, and applications register again what is missing, as [Architecture](./architecture.md#when-redis-loses-writes) explains.

What was lost stays lost, and the Config's history lost it too. The audit log still has each acknowledged write, with its namespace, name and revision: the writes to that namespace above the revision it went back to are the ones to make again.

### When Redis loses everything

If Redis loses everything, the server sets it up again by itself within about 30 seconds, as on a first start: the system namespace, `default`, and the admin from the bootstrap token. It logs the error `The system namespace has no state: the store lost its data.`

So once you have revoked the bootstrap token, as [Security](./security.md#the-first-token) advises, set the variable or Secret to a new token nobody has used and keep that as a break-glass, or remove it: the revoked one would otherwise become the admin again.

The rest is gone: other namespaces, Configs, Roles, RoleBindings, and ServiceAccounts with their tokens. Restore a backup, or create them again and import a [zip export](#configs-as-a-zip-file) of your Configs. With auth on, applications keep serving what they know and stay unregistered until they have a new token. With auth off, they follow what is there once their namespace exists, and register themselves.

## Backing up

### Everything, as an RDB snapshot

An RDB snapshot is everything in Redis at one moment. Have Redis write one, check that it is done, and copy `dump.rdb` from its data directory:

```bash
redis-cli BGSAVE
redis-cli LASTSAVE   # changes once the snapshot is written
```

A Redis Cluster has one per master: back up every master. A managed Redis takes snapshots of its own.

### Configs as a zip file

The [export](./configuration.md#import-and-export) of a namespace holds each Config's name and content. It holds neither its format, labels nor history, nor anything but Configs. It moves between installations and versions, and is readable:

```bash
curl -o prod.zip -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://cosky.example.com/v1/namespaces/prod/configs:export
```

It holds the Configs the token may read, so use one that may read them all. Imported where it does not exist yet, a Config takes the format its extension says: `.yaml` or `.yml`, `.properties`, `.json`, and text for any other. One that exists keeps its format and labels, and takes the new content.

## Restoring

### From an RDB snapshot

Keep at least one server running while you restore. It remembers where each namespace was, and notices that the revision went back.

With AOF on, Redis loads its AOF at start and ignores `dump.rdb`, and with AOF on but no AOF yet, it starts empty. So:

1. Stop Redis.
2. Move its `appendonlydir` aside, and put the snapshot in the data directory as `dump.rdb`.
3. Start Redis with `appendonly no`. It loads the snapshot.
4. Run `redis-cli CONFIG SET appendonly yes`, which writes a new AOF from what Redis holds, and wait for `INFO persistence` to show `aof_rewrite_in_progress:0`.
5. Set `appendonly yes` again where Redis takes its configuration, for its next start.

This was tried on Redis 7.4, with the server running and an application connected. The server logged `Namespace default diverged`, and replaced the epoch. The application took the restored content of its Config at once, and registered its instance again within a renewal, as the instance was newer than the snapshot.

### What a restore means for applications

A restore is Redis losing every write since the snapshot, so it plays out [as above](#when-a-failover-loses-the-last-writes), on every namespace:

- **Configs** go back to what they were, and applications refresh with those values.
- **Instances** registered since are gone, and their processes register them again. Those removed since are back: a leased one goes once its lease expires, a fixed one stays until you remove it again.
- **Leases** in the snapshot have expired by then. Live processes renew theirs, as after any outage, while the reaper's grace and its [mass expiry protection](./architecture.md#leases) keep it from reaping them first.
- **Tokens** created since are gone, and the applications that use them are refused. **A token revoked since is valid again: revoke it again.** Roles and RoleBindings go back too.

If every server restarts along with Redis, none remembers where a namespace was. An application that comes back from a revision beyond the snapshot's is told that its position is gone, and starts over. But one whose revision new writes have already reached may resume on the wrong timeline, and stay there until its periodic fresh snapshot, every 30 minutes or so. That is why a server should keep running through a restore.

### From a zip file

Import it into a namespace that exists:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://cosky.example.com/v1/namespaces/prod/configs:import --data-binary @prod.zip
```

It overwrites Configs of the same name, and leaves the others as they are. Each import is an ordinary write, which applications follow.
</doc>

<doc title="Troubleshooting" path="guide/troubleshooting.md">
# Troubleshooting

This page is for operators of the server. Each entry starts from what you see, a log line, a metric or an error reason, and says what causes it and what to do. [Deployment](./deployment.md#observability) lists the metrics, and [REST API](./rest-api.md#conventions) the error reasons.

## The server does not start

The server says why at the end of its log, under `APPLICATION FAILED TO START`, with a description and an action:

| The description begins | Do |
|---|---|
| `The secret of the bootstrap token, after its second _, has ... characters` | Set `COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` to a new token, such as `cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)`, or remove it. With authentication on, the server checks it at every start, even once it no longer reads it. |
| `The bootstrap token must look like cosky_<id>_<secret>` | The same. |
| `cosky.lease.reaper-interval is 0s: it must be longer than 0.` | A setting that cannot work. The action names the property, its environment variable and its default. A duration without a unit is in seconds. |
| `CoSky cannot reach Redis` | Check `COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI`: the host, the port, the password, and `rediss://` for TLS. |
| `This Redis cannot back CoSky:` | What is wrong follows, such as `maxmemory_policy is allkeys-lru, and eviction silently deletes data; it must be noeviction.` or a version older than 7.0. Change Redis, as [Deployment](./deployment.md#redis) says. A managed Redis may need its parameter group changed. |

One failure ends in a stack trace instead. Look for its last cause:

- **`With an OIDC issuer set, cosky.auth.oidc.audience or client-id is required.`** Set `cosky.auth.oidc.client-id`.

A Redis certificate the JVM does not trust also stops the start: see [Credentials and TLS](./deployment.md#credentials-and-tls).

Three messages come at start without stopping it:

- **`Cannot check the Redis prerequisites, since INFO failed`**: the Redis user may not run `INFO`, so nothing was checked. Give it `+info`.
- **`No RoleBinding exists and no bootstrap token is set, so nobody can sign in.`** Set a [bootstrap token](./security.md#the-first-token) and restart.
- **`Authentication is off (cosky.auth.enabled=false)`**, an error: every caller is admin, and `cosky_auth_enabled` is 0. Turn it on.

An unknown `cosky.*` key stops nothing, so a misspelt property is silently ignored: check the spelling against [Configuration Properties](./properties.md).

## A replica is not ready

The readiness probe, `/actuator/health/readiness`, answers `OUT_OF_SERVICE` with status 503 until the replica has loaded the system namespace, `_system`, and then every namespace it lists. That takes seconds: 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs [took 2 to 3.5](./performance.md). Meanwhile a request for a namespace still loading is refused with `REPLICA_NOT_READY`, and clients go to another replica.

To see what it waits for, set `management.endpoint.health.show-details=always`. The `coSkyReadiness` component of the readiness group then lists those namespaces under `loading`. `_system` alone means the replica has not read the access rules yet, so every call with a token is refused with `REPLICA_NOT_READY` too.

If it stays that way, the replica cannot read Redis. Its log repeats `Following namespace <name> failed; loading it again.` with the cause, and its `cosky_store_failures_total` rises. Check its network path to Redis, and Redis itself.

A replica that is ready stays ready when Redis goes away. That is the next entry.

## A replica cut off from Redis

A replica stays ready while Redis is away, on purpose: Redis is shared, and a failover would otherwise take every replica out of the Service at once. So a replica cut off on its own keeps serving what it last knew. Its reads answer from that, and its writes fail with `STORE_UNAVAILABLE`.

It shows as:

- `rate(cosky_store_failures_total[1m]) > 0` on that replica, even when it is idle, since its reaper asks Redis for a lock every second;
- its `cosky_cache_revision{namespace}` staying behind the other replicas';
- `Reading the log of namespace <name> failed; trying again` in its log.

If one replica shows it, its own path to Redis is broken: restart it, or move it to another node. If every replica shows it, Redis itself is down or failing over, which is the next entry.

## Writes fail with STORE_UNAVAILABLE

`STORE_UNAVAILABLE` (503) means that the server could not reach Redis, or that Redis did not answer within 5 seconds. Reads go on from the replicas' memory. Applications keep their registrations, and renew them once Redis answers again. The reaper then waits 30 seconds before it removes anything, so that they can.

`cosky_store_failures_total{operation}` says what failed: `apply` for writes, `tryLock` for the reaper's lock. The usual causes:

- **Redis is down, or failing over.** A failover of a Cluster or Sentinel took [10 to 16 seconds](./performance.md#a-redis-cluster-failover) when measured.
- **`min-replicas-to-write` on a primary without its replicas.** Redis refuses writes until one is back, as it should: see [Backup and Restore](./backup.md#what-redis-must-do). `INFO replication` on the primary shows the replicas it has.
- **Redis at `maxmemory`.** With `noeviction`, Redis refuses writes rather than drop anything. Give it more memory, or see [Sizing](./deployment.md#sizing) for what takes it.

## Errors that answer 503 or 504

| Reason | Means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `STORE_UNAVAILABLE` | Redis cannot be reached, or did not answer within 5 seconds | See [the entry above](#writes-fail-with-store-unavailable). |
| `REPLICA_NOT_READY` | This replica is still loading the namespace the error names, or is behind the position a client asked for. `_system` stands for the access rules. | Nothing, if it passes: clients go to another replica. If one replica keeps answering it, see [A replica is not ready](#a-replica-is-not-ready). |
| `IDENTITY_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE` | The OIDC provider, or its keys, cannot be reached. The token may be fine. | Check the provider, and the server's way to the issuer. Applications with ServiceAccount tokens go on; sign in with such a token meanwhile. |
| `REVISION_REGRESSION` | Redis lost writes, and the replica is loading the namespace again | It passes in moments. See [Redis lost writes](#redis-lost-writes). |
| `MIN_REVISION_TIMEOUT` (504) | A read with `minRevision` waited 3 seconds for this replica to reach that revision | The replica is behind: check its `cosky_cache_lag_seconds`, and whether it is [cut off from Redis](#a-replica-cut-off-from-redis). |

The four reasons of 503 mean the same to a client: try another replica, or try later. They differ to tell you whether to look at Redis, the identity provider or the replica.

## Calls refused for their token

`cosky_auth_failures_total{reason}` counts them. Each is also a line in the [audit log](./security.md#audit), with the result `UNAUTHENTICATED` and the caller's address in `remote`.

| Reason | Means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `missing` | No token | Find the caller by `remote`: an application without `cosky.token`, or a script. |
| `invalid` | A token that is malformed, unknown, revoked or expired, or an ID token the OIDC checks refuse | Usually a token revoked or rotated while still in use. |
| `unavailable` | It could not be decided: the access rules are loading, or the identity provider is out of reach | It comes with an outage, which `REPLICA_NOT_READY` on `_system` or `IDENTITY_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE` shows. |

An application whose token is refused does not start. It ends with `CoSky refused to register service <name> in namespace <namespace>: UNAUTHENTICATED`. One whose token is revoked while it runs loses its streams, and stays `DEGRADED`.

`PERMISSION_DENIED` (403) is not counted there: the token is valid, and its roles do not allow the call. `GET /v1/me` with that token shows the rules it has.

## Applications stay DEGRADED

The starter's health indicator `cosky` stays `UP`, with `connection: DEGRADED`, while the client is not connected to a server, because a restart would not help. The application serves what it knows meanwhile. Its log says why at each attempt: `The watch stream to <endpoint> failed:`, followed by the status.

| The status | Cause |
|---|---|
| `UNAVAILABLE: io exception (Connection refused ...)` | Nothing listens at `cosky.endpoints`. The port is the gRPC one, 9090, not 8080. |
| `UNAUTHENTICATED` | The token was revoked or has expired: see [the entry above](#calls-refused-for-their-token). |
| `UNAVAILABLE: This replica cannot load namespace <namespace> from its store.`, or one that `has not loaded` it or `is behind` | The replica is [not ready](#a-replica-is-not-ready), or behind. The client opens a new connection, which a Kubernetes Service may route to another replica. |

The client backs off up to 10 seconds between attempts. A server with [TLS](./security.md#tls) needs `cosky.tls.enabled` in the application.

## An application starts with old values

The client keeps a [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) of what it watches in `~/.cosky`, and starts from it, `DEGRADED`, until it reaches a server. A read waits up to a second for the server to answer, so it serves what its last run saw only while no server answers, or one answers slower than that: a Config's old content, or an old list of instances. An empty list fails a call by that service's name. Once connected, it follows the server, and a refresh replaces the old values.

Snapshots are kept per set of endpoints and token. So a development server at the same address as the one before, such as `localhost:9090`, finds the applications starting from what the earlier one served, though it kept nothing. To start clean, delete `~/.cosky`, or set `cosky.snapshot.enabled=false`.

## An application cannot write its snapshots

The client writes its snapshots under `~/.cosky`, and a container user often has no home it may write to. Where that default directory cannot be written, snapshots are off: the application logs once, at info level, `Snapshots are off: the default directory ... cannot be written`, and nothing else is wrong. It serves from memory, and reads the server again after a restart. A directory set with `cosky.snapshot.dir` that cannot be written is warned about instead, once: `Could not write the snapshot <path>: ...`, with the reason, such as `AccessDeniedException`.

To keep snapshots, give it a directory it may write, such as a mounted volume, with `cosky.snapshot.dir` (`COSKY_SNAPSHOT_DIR`). To be rid of the warning about a directory set on purpose, turn snapshots off with `cosky.snapshot.enabled=false` (`COSKY_SNAPSHOT_ENABLED=false`). In Kubernetes a snapshot outlives a restart only on a persistent volume, so a pod without one loses nothing without them. Once a directory set on purpose can be written, the client says `Writes snapshots under ... again`, with no restart.

## Clients start over: cosky_watch_gone_total rises

A client that cannot resume where it was reads a fresh snapshot of what it watches. That costs a read, and loses nothing. The reason says why:

- **`slow`**: it fell out of the window while following, because delivery could not keep up.
- **`compacted`**: it came back from a revision older than the window, as after a reconnection during a rolling update.
- **`epoch`**: the namespace's timeline was replaced, because Redis lost writes or data, or the namespace was deleted and created again.
- **`regression`**: it came back from a position Redis no longer has.

For `slow` and `compacted`, the window is too small for your rate of writes and your reconnection gaps. Raise `cosky.watch.window`, 10,000 events by default, to at least the peak events per second times the longest reconnection gap in seconds, and `cosky.watch.window-bytes` too if your Configs are large. Both also bound the log in Redis, so Redis and each replica keep more: see [Sizing](./deployment.md#sizing). [Performance](./performance.md#the-event-window) shows when it happens.

For `epoch` and `regression`, the window is not the cause: see [Redis lost writes](#redis-lost-writes).

## Reaping is paused

`cosky_lease_protection_active{namespace}` is 1, and the log has, as an error, `<n> of <m> leases expired in namespace <namespace>; pausing the reaper.` More than half of the namespace's leases (`cosky.lease.protection-threshold`) expired at once, out of at least 10 (`protection-min-leases`). That looks like a partition between applications and servers, so the reaper keeps their instances rather than remove live ones. Only the reaper's leader reports the gauge: take `max by (namespace)` over the replicas.

Check whether the applications reach the servers: their logs say `Renewing the lease of namespace <namespace> at <endpoint> failed`, and the network or load balancer in front of port 9090 may be the cause. Once they renew, the share falls, and reaping starts again after a grace of 30 seconds.

If the processes really are gone, as on nodes that failed, reaping starts again by itself after `cosky.lease.protection-max-duration`, 5 minutes. Until then their instances stay listed, and callers need retries.

## cosky_reaper_failures_total rises

The store failed on that namespace while the reaper was reaping or checking it. The reaper goes on with the other namespaces, and this one waits out a grace of its own. The log says `The store failed on namespace <namespace>; it waits out a grace, and the others go on.`, and later `The store answers on namespace <namespace> again`.

On a Redis Cluster, look at the shard that holds the namespace, and its failover. [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md#when-things-fail) says how a shard's failure affects reaping. When the store fails as a whole, the log says `A reaper tick failed.` instead.

## Redis lost writes

`cosky_revision_regression_total` rises, and a replica logs as an error `Namespace <namespace> went back from ...; replacing the epoch.` or `Namespace <namespace> diverged, now at ...; loading it again.` Redis lost writes it had acknowledged, in a failover or because an older snapshot was restored.

CoSky replaces the namespace's epoch. Every replica loads the namespace again, every watcher starts over, `cosky_watch_gone_total{reason="epoch"}` rises, and applications register again what is missing. What Redis lost stays lost: [Backup and Restore](./backup.md#when-redis-loses-data) says how to find it.

`The system namespace has no state: the store lost its data.`, as an error, means that Redis lost everything. The server sets it up again as on a first start: see [Backup and Restore](./backup.md#when-redis-loses-everything).
