`cosky_anti_entropy_drift_total` rising, with `<n> objects of namespace <namespace> differ from the store; replacing the epoch.`, means that a replica's view differed from Redis. It should never happen, and recovers as above. Please [report it](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/issues/new/choose) with the log.

## The Dashboard behind a reverse proxy

[Dashboard](./dashboard.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy) says what the proxy needs. Each missing piece has its own symptom:

| You see | The proxy |
|---|---|
| A blank page, or its files not found, at `/cosky` | Does not redirect `/cosky` to `/cosky/`, so the browser resolves the page's addresses against `/` |
| The page, but every call fails with 404 | Does not pass `/cosky/v1/` on to the server's `/v1/` |
| Changes only after a reload | Buffers responses, which holds back the stream of changes. In nginx, `proxy_buffering off`. |
| Calls blocked by CORS, with the files served from elsewhere | Serves the API from another origin than the page. The server has no CORS, so serve `v1/` next to the page. |

After signing in with OIDC, the provider returns to the address it was given. Register the Dashboard's address with its trailing slash, such as `https://example.com/cosky/`.
</doc>

<doc title="Upgrading" path="guide/upgrading.md">
# Upgrading

This page is for those who run CoSky 8.x and move to a later 8.x release. To move from 6.x, which shares nothing with 8.0, see [Moving from 6.x](./upgrade-8.md).

## What stays compatible

From `8.0.0-rc.1` on, these only grow:

- the gRPC API, error reasons included;
- REST;
- the Kotlin API of `cosky-api`, `cosky-client` and `cosky-spring-boot-starter`;
- the properties of the server and the starter;
- the metrics in [Deployment](./deployment.md#observability), with their labels;
- the data in Redis.

A field, call, property or metric may be added, but none is removed, renumbered, renamed or given another meaning. On every pull request, CI holds the protos, the Kotlin API, REST, the properties and the metrics to this. What `cosky-api` marks `@InternalCoSkyApi`, and the Kotlin API of the other modules, may change in any release. A new major version, such as 9.0, may change anything, and comes with an upgrade guide. [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#releases-and-versioning) has the whole rule.

The alphas and betas made no such promise. Each one's notes say how to upgrade from the one before.

The promise runs one way: a later server reads what an earlier one wrote, and serves earlier applications. Going back to an earlier release is not part of it, so read the notes of the release you leave first.

## In what order

1. **Read the release notes** of each release from yours to the new one, on the [releases page](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/releases). Their section "Upgrading from …" says what to do, and "Known limits" what to expect.
2. **Upgrade the servers**, one replica at a time. The Dashboard comes with them.
3. **Then the applications**, at their own pace: raise `cosky-bom`, build and deploy them as usual.

During a rolling update, replicas of both releases share Redis and serve clients side by side. In Kubernetes, set the new tag, as `newTag` in your overlay's `kustomization.yaml`, and apply it: the Deployment replaces one pod at a time, and clients reconnect to the others and resume where they were, as [Rolling updates](./deployment.md#rolling-updates) explains. With Docker, replace one container at a time, and wait for the new one to be ready before the next.

While it runs, `cosky_watch_gone_total` shows clients that had to read a fresh snapshot instead of resuming, and [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md#clients-start-over-cosky-watch-gone-total-rises) says what to do if it rises.

## From an 8.0 beta to rc.1

rc.1 settled what the promise keeps, so it changed more than a beta did. The data in Redis is unchanged: upgrade the servers in place, then the applications, in one window. A beta application and an rc.1 server, or the reverse, end a watch whose position is gone in ways the other does not know, and such a watch only starts again when the application restarts.

What to check, in short:

- **The bootstrap token**: the server refuses to start with one that is malformed, or whose secret has fewer than 22 characters.
- **Settings**: the server refuses to start with one that cannot work, and a duration without a unit is now in seconds, not milliseconds.
- **Access**: an account that writes Roles, RoleBindings or tokens must hold what it grants.
- **The starter's health indicator** is now `cosky`, switched off by `management.health.cosky.enabled`.
- **Alerts and dashboards**: new values of `cosky_auth_failures_total{reason}`, `max by (namespace)` for `cosky_lease_active`, and a `namespace` label on `cosky_lease_expired_total`.
- **The Kubernetes manifests** put Actuator on port 8081, so scrape the pods there, and request 2Gi of memory.
- **The image** runs as `999:999`, and `JAVA_OPTS` adds to its JVM flags instead of replacing them.
- **REST and gRPC clients of your own**: stricter requests, paged views and a new way a watch ends.
- **OIDC**: register the Dashboard's address with a trailing slash.

The [release notes of rc.1](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/releases/tag/v8.0.0-rc.1) give the details of each. From an earlier beta, read the notes of each release in turn: the data in Redis carries over from beta.1 on.
</doc>

<doc title="Moving from 6.x" path="guide/upgrade-8.md">
# Moving from 6.x

CoSky 8.0 is a new system, and nothing from 6.x carries over by itself. Applications on 6.x talk to Redis directly, and applications on 8.0 talk to the server, so **neither generation can see the other's instances**. There is no bridge: applications move together, in one cutover.

If some services must call each other across generations during a move, run the two installations side by side and switch traffic between whole environments.

## What changes

| | 6.x | 8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Applications reach | Redis, directly | The server, over gRPC |
| Authentication of applications | None | A token on every call |
| Starters | `cosky-spring-cloud-starter-config`, `cosky-spring-cloud-starter-discovery` | `cosky-spring-boot-starter` |
| Loading configuration | `bootstrap.yaml` | `spring.config.import` |
| Settings | `spring.cloud.cosky.*`, `spring.data.redis.*` | `cosky.*` |
| Namespaces | Any name, often `{dev}` or `cosky-{default}` | DNS labels, such as `dev` or `default` |
| Service names | Anything | DNS-style names, lowercase |
| Config formats | Guessed from the extension | Declared with the Config |
| Staying alive | Each instance's own TTL | One lease per process |
| Applications without a web server | Registered, given `registry.port` | Do not register by themselves: call the client's `instances.register` |
| Taking an instance out of rotation | `ServiceRegistry.setStatus` | A weight of `0` |
| People | Users with passwords | OIDC, or ServiceAccount tokens |
| Permissions | Read or write per namespace | Roles down to kinds, verbs and name prefixes |
| Audit | A page in the Dashboard | JSON lines in the log |
| Redis | Any version | 7.0 or later, `noeviction` |
| JDK | 17 | 21 for clients, 25 for the server |

## What moves

| | How |
|---|---|
| Configs, with their history if you like | `cosky-migrate` |
| Instances that register themselves | They do so on 8.0 when they switch |
| Fixed instances | By hand, from the report |
| Users and roles | By hand, from the report |
| Audit log and topology | They do not. The audit log stays in 6.x's Redis, and topology rebuilds itself. |

Revisions and timestamps start anew. A Config removed in 6.x has no current version, and does not arrive.

## Getting the tool

Each [release](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/releases) carries `cosky-migrate` as a zip file. Unpack it, and run `bin/cosky-migrate` with JDK 21 or later.

To build it instead, with JDK 21 installed:

```bash
./gradlew :migration:installDist
```

The tool is then at `migration/build/install/cosky-migrate/bin/cosky-migrate`.

## The cutover

**1. Start 8.0.** It may share the Redis of 6.x if that Redis meets the [requirements](./requirements.md): their keys do not overlap.

**2. Rehearse while 6.x still runs.** This reads both sides, writes nothing, and writes a report:

```bash
export COSKY_TOKEN=<bootstrap token>
cosky-migrate --source redis://6x-redis:6379 --target http://cosky:8080 --dry-run
```

Read `cosky-migration-report.md`:

- **Service names to change.** `OrderService` cannot register on 8.0, so change `spring.application.name`.
- **Namespaces 8.0 cannot name.** `cosky-{default}` goes to `default` and `{dev}` to `dev`, while anything else illegal stops the run. Name it with `--namespace 'Old_Name=new-name'`, or leave it out with `--namespace 'Old_Name='`. A namespace 6.x never listed must be named this way too.
- **Configs 8.0 refuses**, such as a name holding `:` or content over 1 MiB.

**3. Rebuild people and permissions.** The report lists every 6.x role with the 8.0 rule each grant corresponds to, and every user with their roles. Create those roles and bindings, and a ServiceAccount with a token for each application. An application without a token cannot do anything on a server with auth on.

**4. Prepare the applications.** Replace the starters, move `bootstrap.yaml` into `application.yaml`, and set the token. The applications run on Spring Boot 4.2 and Spring Cloud 2026.0:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  config:
    import: "cosky:order-service.yaml"
cosky:
  endpoints: cosky.internal:9090
  token: ${COSKY_TOKEN}
  namespace: prod
```

**5. Stop writing Configs to 6.x, and import.**

```bash
cosky-migrate --source redis://6x-redis:6379 --target http://cosky:8080 --history
```

Exit code `0` means everything arrived, `1` that some Configs need attention, and `2` that it could not run or stopped early. Running it again continues an interrupted run, and changes nothing else, except the format of Configs named without an extension when `--default-format` is another than before: those it imported and nobody edited on 8.0 since, listed in the report.

**6. Switch.** Deploy the applications on 8.0 and stop 6.x. Then create the fixed instances from the report: nothing renews them, so nothing registers them again.

## What the tool will not do

- **Overwrite an edit.** A Config whose content on 8.0 matches no version left in 6.x was edited there, so it stays and is reported. To import it anyway, delete it on 8.0 first.
- **Touch 6.x.** It only reads, and never reads a password hash.
- **Copy secrets into the report.** It holds names, addresses and permissions, never the content of a Config or a metadata value.

For a Redis password, use `COSKY_SOURCE_URI` rather than `--source`, where `ps` cannot see it. Run `cosky-migrate --help` for everything else.

## Going back

Until you stop 6.x, going back is deploying the applications on 6.x again. Nothing writes to its keys, but Configs edited on 8.0 after the switch stay on 8.0.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration Properties" path="guide/properties.md">
# Configuration Properties

A duration takes a unit, such as `500ms`, `30s` or `5m`. Without one it is in seconds, on the server and in the starter alike, so `COSKY_LEASE_REAPER_GRACE=30` is 30 seconds. Both ship Spring Boot's configuration metadata, so an IDE completes and explains the `cosky.*` properties below.

## Server

Set these in `application.yaml`, as arguments, or as environment variables: `cosky.store.redis.uri` is `COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI`.

A value that cannot work stops the start, with a message that names the property and the value:

- a duration, count or size of 0 or less. `reaper-grace` and `protection-max-duration` may be 0, which turns the grace or the pause off, as may `protection-min-leases`;
- a `protection-threshold` outside 0 to 1;
- a `lock-ttl` no longer than `reaper-interval`: the lock would lapse between two renewals, and leadership change hands.

Keys the server does not know are ignored, such as `COSKY_SERVICE_HOST` and `COSKY_PORT`, which Kubernetes sets for a Service named `cosky`.

### Store

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.store.type` | `redis` | `redis`, or `memory` for development: nothing survives the process |
| `cosky.store.redis.uri` | `redis://localhost:6379` | Also takes Sentinel URIs, such as `redis-sentinel://s1:26379,s2:26379#mymaster`: the server follows the master the Sentinels name. A command waits at most 5 seconds for Redis, unless the URI sets its own, such as `?timeout=10s` |
| `cosky.store.redis.cluster` | `false` | The URI is a seed of a Redis Cluster |
| `cosky.store.redis.tail-poll-interval` | `1s` | How often each namespace is read when no hint arrives |

### Authentication

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.auth.enabled` | `true` | Off, everyone may do everything. Only for development: on Redis the server logs an error at start, and `cosky_auth_enabled` is 0. |
| `cosky.auth.bootstrap-token` | `$COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` | Becomes the `admin` ServiceAccount while no role binding exists. Its secret takes at least 22 letters and digits, see [Security](./security.md#the-first-token) |
| `cosky.auth.namespace-accounts` | `true` | Gives every namespace a ServiceAccount of its own name, bound to `client` there, whose token its applications share |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.issuer` | — | Turns OIDC on, together with `client-id` |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.client-id` | — | The Dashboard's client |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.audience` | The client | What a token must be for |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.groups-claim` | `groups` | The claim holding group names |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.scopes` | `openid, profile` | What the Dashboard asks for. Some providers send groups only when asked. |

### Watch and reads

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.watch.window` | `10000` | Events kept for resuming, and in the store's log. Should be at least the peak event rate times the longest reconnection gap. |
| `cosky.watch.window-bytes` | `64MB` | The same in bytes, per namespace, in memory and in the store's log. |
| `cosky.watch.progress-interval` | `10s` | Bookmarks sent on idle watches |
| `cosky.watch.max-per-stream` | `1000` | Watches on one stream |
| `cosky.watch.anti-entropy-interval` | `5m` | How often a replica compares its view with the store |
| `cosky.read.min-revision-timeout` | `3s` | How long a read or a resume waits for a replica to catch up |
| `cosky.view.topology-flush-interval` | `30s` | How often a replica records who watches whom. Edges expire after three times this. |

### Leases

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.lease.reaper-interval` | `1s` | How often expired leases are looked for |
| `cosky.lease.reaper-grace` | `30s` | No reaping for this long after becoming leader, or after failing to reach the store; a failure in one namespace holds back that namespace only |
| `cosky.lease.reaper-max-per-tick` | `100` | Leases reaped per namespace per round |
| `cosky.lease.lock-ttl` | `15s` | How long the reaper's leadership lasts without renewal |
| `cosky.lease.protection-threshold` | `0.5` | Reaping pauses when more than this share of a namespace's leases expire at once |
| `cosky.lease.protection-min-leases` | `10` | Namespaces with fewer leases have no such pause |
| `cosky.lease.protection-max-duration` | `5m` | How long the pause lasts at most |

### From Spring

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server.port` | `8080` | REST, Dashboard and Actuator |
| `management.server.port` | `server.port` | Actuator on [a port of its own](./deployment.md#actuator-on-its-own-port), as in `k8s/base` |
| `spring.grpc.server.port` | `9090` | gRPC |
| `server.ssl.bundle`, `spring.grpc.server.ssl.bundle` | — | [TLS](./security.md#tls) |
| `spring.grpc.server.shutdown.grace-period` | `5s` | How long open streams get on shutdown |
| `spring.grpc.server.keepalive.connection.max-age` | `30m` | A client connection is ended after this, give or take a tenth, so that clients [spread over the replicas again](./deployment.md#rolling-updates) |
| `spring.grpc.server.keepalive.connection.grace-period` | `5s` | How long the streams of such a connection get |
| `management.tracing.sampling.probability` | `0.1` | Share of requests traced |
| `management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint` | — | Where traces go |
| `springdoc.api-docs.enabled` | `true` | The REST API's document at `/v3/api-docs`, and Swagger UI on it at `/swagger-ui.html`; `springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false` keeps the document only |

### Fixed limits

These cannot be set in 8.0.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Config content | 1 MiB |
| Config history | The last 20 revisions |
| Lease TTL | 5 to 300 seconds, 30 by default |
| Instance metadata | 64 entries; keys up to 63 characters, values up to 1024 |
| Labels | 32 entries; keys up to 63 characters, values up to 253 |
| Description | 1024 characters |
| Tokens per ServiceAccount | 2 |
| One message | 2 MiB; larger results come in pages or parts |
| One page of a list | 500 by default, 1000 at most |
| A REST request's body | 12 MiB, what the largest object takes in JSON with every character escaped; an archive to import 64 MiB |

## Spring Boot starter

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.enabled` | `true` | Everything below |
| `cosky.endpoints` | `localhost:9090` | Servers to try in turn |
| `cosky.token` | — | Sent on every call. A blank one counts as none, so `${COSKY_TOKEN:}` can stand beside `cosky.token-file`. |
| `cosky.token-file` | — | A file holding the token instead, such as a mounted secret. Read again once it changes, so a rotated token needs no restart. |
| `cosky.namespace` | `default` | |
| `cosky.tls.enabled` | `false` | Connect over TLS |
| `cosky.tls.trusted-certificates` | — | A PEM file to trust, for a private CA. The JVM's trust store decides otherwise. |
| `cosky.snapshot.enabled` | `true` | Keep views on disk |
| `cosky.snapshot.dir` | `~/.cosky` | Left as is and not writable, as for a container user without a home, snapshots are off |
| `cosky.snapshot.include-config` | `true` | Snapshots are not encrypted, so false keeps Config contents off the disk |
| `cosky.registry.enabled` | `true` | Register this application |
| `cosky.registry.weight` | `1` | `0` takes no traffic |
| `cosky.registry.metadata` | — | |
| `cosky.discovery.enabled` | `true` | `DiscoveryClient` and LoadBalancer |
| `cosky.discovery.load-timeout` | `5s` | How long the first read of a service waits |
| `cosky.config.load-timeout` | `5s` | How long importing a Config waits |
| `cosky.config.refresh.enabled` | `true` | Publish `RefreshEvent` on changes |
| `management.health.cosky.enabled` | `true` | The health indicator, `cosky` in `/actuator/health` |

The service name is `spring.application.name`. `spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled: false` also stops registering.

An application's own bean takes the place of the starter's: one named `coskyHealthIndicator`, or one of type `CoSkyDiscoveryClient`, `CoSkyReactiveDiscoveryClient`, `CoSkyServiceRegistry` or `CoSkyAutoServiceRegistration`.
</doc>

<doc title="REST API" path="guide/rest-api.md">
# REST API

The management API, on port 8080. Its OpenAPI 3.1 document has the same schemas as gRPC, since both come from one set of protos. A server serves it at `/v3/api-docs` (`/v3/api-docs.yaml` as YAML), and shows it in Swagger UI at `/swagger-ui.html`, where **Authorize** takes a token. `./gradlew :api:generateOpenApi` writes it to `api/build/openapi/cosky.yaml`, with the item schema of the Watch's event stream as well, which the server's copy leaves out.

## Conventions

**Authentication**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, on everything except `GET /v1/auth/config` and [Actuator](./security.md#what-is-not-protected).

**Resources** have shared metadata and one kind-specific spec, in proto3 JSON. Empty fields are left out, and 64-bit numbers such as revisions are strings.

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "namespace": "prod",
    "name": "app.yaml",
    "revision": "42",
    "createRevision": "7",
    "updatedAt": "2026-08-18T01:00:00Z",
    "updatedBy": "serviceaccount:admin"
  },
  "config": {"format": "CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML", "content": "a: 1", "sha256": "..."}
}
```

**Names**: `{name}` is one path segment, so a `/` in a Config name is sent as `%2F`.

**Writes** replace the whole object, and read-only fields are ignored. A body may leave out `meta.namespace` and `meta.name`, but not name another place than the path. A member the object does not have is refused with `400` rather than dropped: a misspelt `lables` would otherwise clear the labels.

| Header | Means |
|---|---|
| `If-Match: "42"` | Only if it is still at revision 42 |
| `If-None-Match: *` | Only if it does not exist. It takes nothing but `*`, and not together with `If-Match` |

A write whose condition fails answers `409` `REVISION_CONFLICT`, not the `412` of RFC 9110, as Kubernetes does: it is a conflict of revisions, with the same reason and the same detail as over gRPC.

`GET` and `PUT` return the revision as `ETag`. A `PUT` of what is already there answers `{"changed": false}` and creates no revision; its `revision` and `ETag` are those the object has, good for the next `If-Match`. A `DELETE` of what is not there answers `deleted` false, with the namespace's revision. Either answer's `revision` is good for `minRevision`.

**Lists** come in pages: pass `nextPageToken` as `pageToken` until it is empty. `pageSize` is 500 by default and 1000 at most, and a page can hold fewer when the objects are large. The response's `revision` and `epoch` let you start a Watch from where the list ended.

**Reading your own writes**: a replica may be slightly behind. `?minRevision=42` waits until it has reached that revision, and answers `504` after 3 seconds.

**Violations** in a `400` name the field as gRPC does, by its proto path in the request: a parameter or header by the field it sets (`pageSize` is `page_size`, `labelSelector` is `label_selector`, `minRevision` is `min_revision`, `If-Match` and `If-None-Match` are `expected_revision`, `toRevision` is `to_revision`, `expiresAt` is `expires_at`, the Watch's `kind` is `create.kind`), and a body by the field it carries: `resource` for a `PUT`, and the path of a member it does not have, such as `resource.meta.lables`.

**A body** may take 12 MiB, what the largest object takes in JSON with every character escaped, and an archive to import 64 MiB. A larger one is refused with `400`, a `VIOLATION_CODE_TOO_LONG` on the field the body carries, before the server reads the rest of it.

**Errors** are problem details ([RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)), as `application/problem+json`. Beside `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, `code` is the gRPC status, and `reason` the reason, which does not change between versions. Some reasons add a member that says more. `type` leads to the reason's row below.

```json
{
  "type": "https://cosky.ahoo.me/guide/rest-api#revision-conflict",
  "title": "Revision conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "KIND_CONFIG prod/app.yaml: expected revision 42, current revision 43.",
  "instance": "/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/app.yaml",
  "code": "ABORTED",
  "reason": "ERROR_REASON_REVISION_CONFLICT",
  "revisionConflict": {
    "key": {"namespace": "prod", "kind": "KIND_CONFIG", "name": "app.yaml"},
    "expectedRevision": "42",
    "currentRevision": "43"
  }
}
```

| Reason | HTTP | More |
|---|---|---|
| <a id="resource-not-found"></a>`RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `resourceNotFound`: the key |
| <a id="namespace-not-found"></a>`NAMESPACE_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `namespace` |
| <a id="invalid-argument"></a>`INVALID_ARGUMENT` | 400 | `badRequest`: the violations |
| <a id="unauthenticated"></a>`UNAUTHENTICATED` | 401 |  |
| <a id="permission-denied"></a>`PERMISSION_DENIED` | 403 |  |
| <a id="revision-conflict"></a>`REVISION_CONFLICT` | 409 | `revisionConflict`: the key, the expected and the current revision |
| <a id="namespace-not-empty"></a>`NAMESPACE_NOT_EMPTY` | 409 | `namespace` |
| <a id="lease-not-found"></a>`LEASE_NOT_FOUND` | 412 | `leaseNotFound` |
| <a id="watch-quota-exceeded"></a>`WATCH_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | 429 | `watchQuotaExceeded`: the limit |
| <a id="store-unavailable"></a>`STORE_UNAVAILABLE` | 503 | The store cannot be reached |
| <a id="identity-provider-unavailable"></a>`IDENTITY_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE` | 503 | The OIDC provider or its keys cannot be reached; the token may be fine |
| <a id="replica-not-ready"></a>`REPLICA_NOT_READY` | 503 | `namespace`: this server is still loading it, or is behind; another may answer |
| <a id="revision-regression"></a>`REVISION_REGRESSION` | 503 | `namespace` |
| <a id="min-revision-timeout"></a>`MIN_REVISION_TIMEOUT` | 504 | `namespace` |

Failures that are not CoSky's own, such as a path that does not exist, are problem details too, of the type `about:blank`, without `code` or `reason`.

## Endpoints

### Configs

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs` | List. `?labelSelector=a%3D1&labelSelector=b%3D2`: one `key=value` to each, all of which must match. Nothing is split at commas, which a value may hold |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}` | |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}/history` | Newest first. `?limit=` is the most revisions over all pages together, and `?pageToken=` the next page |
| POST | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}:rollback` | `{"toRevision": "41"}`. Writes that content as a new revision, and brings back a deleted Config. A revision the history does not hold is a `400` on `to_revision`. |
| POST | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs:import` | A zip file as the body; each entry path is a Config name |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs:export` | A zip file |

### Instances

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/instances` | List. `?service=order&labelSelector=zone%3Deast` |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/instances/{name}` | Without `meta.lease`, it stays until deleted. The service cannot change |

Leases are gRPC only: applications use the [client](./sdk.md).

### Watch

`GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/watch?kind=KIND_CONFIG&name=&service=&fromRevision=&fromEpoch=`

`kind` takes the enum names. Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, Roles and RoleBindings are watched in `_system`: `/v1/namespaces/_system/watch?kind=KIND_ROLE`.

Server-sent events, one proto3 JSON message per `data:` line:

| Message | Means |
|---|---|
| `snapshot` | The current state, when `fromRevision` is 0. Holds the `epoch` to resume with. |
| `events` | One revision's changes |
| `progress` | A bookmark, every 10 seconds while idle |
| `positionGone` | Your position is no longer valid, and the stream ends: start over without one. It holds the `earliestRevision` and `epoch` there are now, and the `reason`: `GONE_REASON_COMPACTED` (older than the window), `GONE_REASON_SLOW` (fell out of it), `GONE_REASON_EPOCH` (another timeline), `GONE_REASON_REGRESSION` (a lost one) or `GONE_REASON_PERMISSION` (what you may see changed). Start over whatever the reason, also for one added later |
| `canceled` | The stream ends, for the reason given |

Large snapshots and revisions span several messages, marked by `more`. An `EventSource` cannot send a token: use `fetch` with a stream reader, as the Dashboard does.

### Views

Computed from the server's memory, read-only. Services and the topology come in pages like lists, by `pageSize` and `pageToken`; without `pageSize` everything comes in as few pages as the size limit allows, usually one.

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/services` | Services and their instance counts |
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/topology` | Who consumes whom |
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/stats` | Counts of services, instances and Configs |

### Global objects

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{name}` | The smallest body is `{"namespace":{}}`. Only an empty namespace can be deleted. While a deletion is under way, `namespace.terminating` is `true`, `namespace.terminatingEpoch` names the namespace it is for, and a write gets `404`. A deletion that finds the namespace created again meanwhile stops with `409` and changes nothing. |
| GET | `/v1/serviceaccounts` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}` | The smallest body is `{"serviceAccount":{}}`. `tokens` in the body is ignored. |
| POST | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}/tokens` | Returns the plaintext once, with the account's new `revision`. `{"expiresAt": "..."}` is optional. |
| DELETE | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}/tokens/{tokenId}` | Answers `{"revision", "deleted"}`; a token the account does not hold is `deleted` false, not an error. Both token calls take `If-Match` with the account's revision. |
| GET | `/v1/roles` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/roles/{name}` | |
| GET | `/v1/rolebindings` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/rolebindings/{name}` | |

### Identity

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/v1/me` | Who you are, and your effective rules |
| `/v1/auth/config` | How people sign in. Needs no token and holds public values only. |

### Operations

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/actuator/health/liveness`, `/actuator/health/readiness` | Probes |
| `/actuator/prometheus` | [Metrics](./deployment.md#observability) |
</doc>

<doc title="Requirements" path="guide/requirements.md">
# Requirements

| Component | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Server | JDK 25 | The image includes it |
| Client and starter | JDK 21 or later | |
| `cosky-migrate` | JDK 21 or later | |
| Building from source | JDK 21 and JDK 25 | Gradle does not download them |
| Spring Boot | 4.2.0 | For the starter, which is built and tested on it. A release that manages an older gRPC than the client is built on mixes gRPC versions, which fails at runtime |
| Spring Cloud | 2026.0 | Declares Spring Boot 4.2, so its compatibility verifier can stay on |
| Redis | 7.0 or later, Redis 8 included, with `maxmemory-policy noeviction` | The server checks both at start, and refuses to run otherwise |
| Valkey | 8 | |
| Kubernetes | 1.27 or later, with Kustomize | The manifests use `matchLabelKeys` and `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy`, on by default from 1.27, and meet Pod Security's "restricted" level. CI deploys them to k3s 1.31 for every pull request. |
| Browser | A current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari | Only Chrome is tested |

Every pull request runs against Redis 7.0, Redis 7.4, Redis 8.12 and Valkey 8, on a single node and a Redis Cluster.

## Dependencies

| Library | Version |
|---|---|
| Kotlin | 2.4, compiled to Java 21. Compiling against it takes Kotlin 2.3 or later. |
| gRPC | 1.84 |
| Protobuf | 4.36 |
| Spring gRPC | 1.1 |
| Lettuce | 7.5 |

`cosky-bom` manages the versions of the CoSky modules. Spring Boot's and Spring Cloud's own BOMs manage the rest.
</doc>

<doc title="Architecture" path="guide/architecture.md">
# Architecture

This page explains how CoSky works and what it guarantees. The [design document](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) has the reasoning behind each decision.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Apps["Applications"]
        A1["Local view<br>+ snapshot on disk"]
    end
    subgraph Server["CoSky server replicas"]
        API["gRPC and REST"] --> CACHE["Watch cache<br>per namespace"]
        REAPER["Lease reaper<br>one leader"]
    end
    REDIS[("Redis<br>objects + change log")]
    A1 -- "Put, leases" --> API
    CACHE -- "Watch" --> A1
    API -- "atomic write" --> REDIS
    REDIS -- "change log" --> CACHE
    REAPER --> REDIS
```

## The data model

Everything is a **Resource**: shared metadata and one spec. A Namespace, Config, Instance, ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding are all handled by one API.

A **namespace** is the unit of everything: of isolation, of ordering, and of placement, since it stays in one Redis slot. Each has its own **revision**, a counter that goes up by one with each write. An object remembers the revision that last changed it.

Global kinds live in the reserved namespace `_system`.

## A write

1. The server validates the request and checks permission.
2. One Lua script, atomically: compares the expected revision if asked, gives the namespace its next revision, stores the object, and appends the change to the namespace's log, a Redis Stream.
3. The write is acknowledged.

Writing what is already there changes nothing, and creates no revision.

## Following changes

Each replica follows each namespace's log, and keeps an immutable view of the namespace in memory, plus a window of recent changes. A write publishes a hint, so followers usually read at once. Should a hint be lost, each also polls once a second.

Watchers read those views without any lock. A slow watcher only misses intermediate views, then finds what it missed in the window. It holds back nobody else. If it falls out of the window, it gets `gone` and starts over from a snapshot of what it watches, which is the only cost.

So Redis load grows with the number of namespaces and replicas, and not with the number of clients. [Performance](./performance.md#many-namespaces-and-a-redis-cluster) measures it, on one Redis and on a Cluster.

Every 5 minutes, a replica also compares its view with the store. Any difference should be impossible, so it counts as a lost timeline, as below.

## What a client can rely on

- **Order**: changes within a namespace arrive in revision order, and a whole revision at once. Subscribers never see half of one.
- **Delivery**: exactly once within a stream. Across reconnections at least once, and the client drops what it already applied.
- **Resuming**: a client that reconnects to any replica continues from the revision it saw.
- **Reads** are from a local view, so they can be slightly stale. Propagation was [measured](./performance.md) at under 200 ms to 5,000 connections.
- **Writes** go to the primary, and are atomic. `minRevision` lets a REST caller read its own write from any replica.

As a safety net, a client also starts over from a fresh snapshot every 30 minutes or so.

## Leases

A process holds one lease per namespace, and attaches its instances to it, so renewing costs the same however many it has. An Instance without a lease is simply permanent, with no special handling.

One replica at a time runs the **reaper**, under a lock in Redis, which a stopping replica gives up so that another takes over at once rather than when the lock expires. It removes the instances of expired leases, with these protections, because removing live instances is worse than keeping dead ones:

1. **Grace**: after becoming leader, or failing to reach the store, it reaps nothing for 30 seconds. Clients have time to reconnect, and an expired lease can still be renewed until it is reaped. When the store fails on one namespace only, such as one on a Redis Cluster shard that is down, only that namespace waits, counting from its last failure, and the others are reaped as usual. A call to a shard fails at once while the connection to it is down; one to a master that hangs with its connection open waits out the 5-second command timeout, which counts as the whole store hanging, until the cluster marks that master as failed.
2. **Delay**: a lease is reaped a third of its TTL after expiry. Leases cut off by one partition expire over that span, since they renew at different moments. Reaping at once would remove them one by one, and the next step would never see them together.
3. **Mass expiry**: when more than half of a namespace's leases have expired, and it has at least 10, reaping pauses and logs an error. This covers a partition between clients and servers, which the grace cannot detect. When the share falls, grace starts over. After 5 minutes, it reaps regardless.
4. **Pace**: at most 100 leases per namespace per round.

The cost is that a process that really crashed stays listed for 40 seconds by default. Callers should retry.

## When Redis loses writes

Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes, and revisions then go backwards or diverge. Each namespace carries an **epoch**, a random value that changes when this is found, and a position is an epoch and a revision together.

| Detected by | Then |
|---|---|
| The log's position going backwards or missing | Every replica reloads, and every watcher gets `gone` and starts over |
| A client resuming from a revision the store does not have | That client gets `gone` |
| A lease that no longer exists | The client registers everything again |
| The periodic comparison with the store | The epoch is replaced, so all of the above follows |

The system returns to a consistent state, but what Redis lost stays lost. It takes an application to restore a Config, from its history or by writing it again.

## When servers are away

An application keeps serving its local view. On restart, it loads the [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) from disk. Without a snapshot and without a server, an import that is not `optional` fails the start, so that an application does not run without its configuration.

## Why a server at all

CoSky 6.x had applications talk to Redis directly, which left the data plane without authentication, tied every client to one storage layout, and grew Redis's connections with the number of processes. Adding one small server gives authentication on every call, clients for any language, and resumable streams, while reads stay local. The server keeps nothing durable itself, so replicas can come and go.

Redis stays because it is what CoSky is for: for those who already run it, there is nothing new to operate. Those who need more durability should use a system built on consensus.
</doc>

<doc title="Performance" path="guide/performance.md">
# Performance

Measured through real gRPC and serialization, with the server in a JVM of its own on JDK 25 with compact object headers, against a Redis 7.4 container. **Load generator and server shared one 10-core laptop, over loopback**, so there was no real network unless [one was emulated](#over-an-emulated-network), and the generator competed with the server for CPU. Treat these as an indication, and measure on your own hardware. The failovers name the release they were measured on; the other figures come from 8.0.0-alpha.1 to 8.0.0-beta.1, and were not measured again for rc.1.

## Results

| Target | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs in a namespace | Written in 7 seconds at 64 concurrent writers. A second replica loaded them and was ready in 2 to 3.5 seconds. | Met |
| About 1 KB per instance | 86 MB for 60,000 objects, about 1.5 KB each, with the index by service and the event window | Slightly over |
| Write p99 under 20 ms | 2 ms at about 12,000 writes per second with 16 writers; 8 ms at most. Over an emulated network with Redis and clients each 6 ms away, 15 ms with one writer. | Met, but not where 1% of packets are lost |
| 20,000 connections and 100,000 watches on a replica | All succeeded, in 7 seconds, and the heap grew by about 370 MB. | Met |
| Propagation p99 under 500 ms | With every write going to every connection: 89 ms to 5,000 connections, 135 ms to 10,000, and 154 to 189 ms to 20,000 in 4 runs, 400 ms at most. Over an emulated network, 348 ms to 5,000 clients 58 ms away that lose 0.5% of packets. | Met |
| `choose()` and reading a Config allocate nothing | `choose()` 24 to 58 million operations per second, reading a Config about 1,500 million, at about 0 bytes each | Met |

Propagation is measured in the worst case: every connection watches the same service, and the generator receives every copy on the same machine. In real traffic, an event goes only to those who depend on that service.

Earlier runs at 20,000 connections sometimes had a tail of 1 to 10 seconds. It came from the generator: its gRPC client ran callbacks on a thread for each busy stream, and some 900 threads competed with the server for the 10 cores, while the server had no GC pause and Redis no slow command. With the callbacks on the transport's threads, the tail went away.

The connection figures come from a Linux container on the same laptop, because on macOS a client runs out of ports at about 16,000 connections. That is what stopped earlier runs at about 15,000. The load generator and the server still share 10 cores.

## The event window

A replica was killed under load, and 100 clients reconnected to another one, all watching one service. Falling out of the window means reading a fresh snapshot of that service, which costs little.

| Writes per second | Window | Clients | Deliveries per second | `gone` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| About 160 | 10,000 | 100 | About 16,000 | 0 |
| About 1,600 | 10,000 | 5 / 20 | About 8,000 / 32,000 | 0 |
| About 1,600 | 10,000 | 100 | About 160,000 | 97 to 100 |
| About 1,500 | 50,000 | 100 | About 150,000 | 0 |

So `gone` appears only when delivery cannot keep up, around 160,000 per second. The default stays at 10,000, and `cosky_watch_gone_total` after a rolling update shows whether yours should be larger.

## Large Configs

A server with 512 MB of heap, with one 1 MB Config written over and over:

| Limit in bytes | Writes | Heap | Redis |
|---|---|---|---|
| None | Started failing after about 500 | Reached 510 MB | 509 MB, after 484 |
| 64 MB, in memory only | All 800 succeeded | Steady at about 120 MB | 825 MB, after 800 |
| 64 MB, in memory and in the log | All 800 succeeded | Steady at about 120 MB | 92 MB, after 800 |

It restarted on that log in 4 seconds, and took 50 more writes. Trimming the log made no visible difference to write speed: in alternating runs, 16 writers reached about 11,400 and 9,600 writes per second, against 11,500 and 10,400 before.

## A Redis Cluster failover

On a cluster of three masters and three replicas in Docker, with a node timeout of 5 seconds, one server wrote a Config every 100 ms to a namespace while its master was stopped:

| The master | The namespace unavailable, 8.0.0-beta.7 |
|---|---|
| Killed (`docker kill`) | 10.5 to 15.8 seconds, in three runs |
| Frozen (`docker pause`) | 15.6 seconds |

That is the node timeout, the replica's election, and then up to 10 seconds: the server reads the topology every 5 seconds, and each read waits up to 5 seconds for the stopped node. How much of those 10 seconds a run takes depends on when the reads fall: of three kills, two were over after 10.5 and 10.6 seconds, one after 15.8. Meanwhile each request on that namespace failed with `STORE_UNAVAILABLE` after 5 seconds. 8.0.0-alpha.5 left it unavailable for 53 seconds after a kill, and after a freeze until the master answered again, as it never read the topology again.

## A Redis Sentinel failover

On a master with one replica and three Sentinels in Docker, which take a master that does not answer for 5 seconds as down, one server wrote a Config every 100 ms while the master was stopped:

| The master | 8.0.0-beta.1 | 8.0.0-beta.2 | 8.0.0-beta.7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Killed (`docker kill`) | 10.2 seconds | 15.5 seconds | 15.5 seconds |
| Frozen (`docker pause`) | Until it answered again: not within 240 seconds | 16.2 seconds | 16.2 seconds |
| Handed over (`SENTINEL FAILOVER`) | At once | At once | At once: no write failed while the Sentinels handed over, 1.1 seconds after |

A plain connection asks the Sentinels for the master only when it connects. A master that hangs keeps its connections open, so beta.1 went on sending to it, and each request failed after a minute. The server now follows what the Sentinels announce, and a request fails with `STORE_UNAVAILABLE` after 5 seconds instead. After a kill, beta.1's first request waited 10.2 seconds and then succeeded, longer than a client waits for a call, 10 seconds; now requests fail after 5 seconds each until the server has followed. A Sentinel that hands the master over closes its clients' connections itself, so both follow at once.

## Many namespaces, and a Redis Cluster

Three replicas followed many namespaces of 50 Instances each, on Redis 7.4 alone and on a Redis Cluster of three masters and three replicas, all in one container on the same laptop. 16 writers wrote 32,000 Configs through one replica, each to a namespace picked at random, and a client on another replica watched 100 of the namespaces.

| | 1,000 namespaces, one Redis | 1,000 namespaces, Cluster | 5,000 namespaces, one Redis | 5,000 namespaces, Cluster |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The second and third replicas ready | 3.3 and 4.0 s | 3.4 and 4.1 s | 4.7 and 6.7 s | 5.2 and 7.5 s |
| Redis at rest | 21,000 commands/s, 11% CPU | 6,700 commands/s and 4% CPU on each master | 129,000 commands/s, 30% CPU | 42,000 commands/s and 11% CPU on each master |
| Writes | 8,354/s, p99 5 ms | 7,809/s, p99 7 ms | 6,739/s, p99 9 ms | 6,240/s, p99 9 ms |
| Redis while writing | 77% CPU | 39 to 43% CPU on each master | 84% CPU | 48 to 55% CPU on each master |
| A write reaching the watcher on another replica, p99 | 14 ms | 23 ms | 8 ms | 16 ms |

At rest, each replica reads each namespace once a second, should a hint have been lost: about seven Redis commands a read. That load grows with the namespaces times the replicas, and not with clients. On one Redis it reached 30% of its CPU at 5,000 namespaces and three replicas; a Cluster spreads it over its masters, and a longer `cosky.store.redis.tail-poll-interval` lowers it, at the cost of a slower recovery from a lost hint.

A write cost about 35 Redis commands with three replicas: the write itself, and one read of the namespace by each replica. In a Cluster, the hint that a write publishes reaches every node, which showed as 4,000 to 5,000 messages a second received by each master, at no visible cost. Here the laptop, not Redis, limited the writes: one Redis was close to saturated, while the masters of the Cluster had half their CPU left.

The targets above, measured again on a Cluster, matched one Redis: one namespace of 50,000 Instances and 10,000 Configs, 17,500 writes per second with 16 writers at p99 2 ms, 5,000 connections watching, propagation p99 103 ms, and a second replica ready in 2.9 seconds.

## Over an emulated network

The targets above, measured again with a network between the server and Redis, and between the clients and the server: 5,000 connections watching, one namespace of 50,000 Instances and 10,000 Configs. Each link is a [Toxiproxy](https://github.com/Shopify/toxiproxy) relay in a container, whose interface `netem` shapes, so that each direction is delayed once. The round trips are measured one request at a time, as `netem` here delays a packet alone on the link by milliseconds more than it is told ([how it was run](#how-it-was-run)).

| | Loopback | Redis and clients 6 ms away | The same, 0.1% of packets lost | 7 ms with jitter, 1% lost | Clients 58 ms away, 0.5% lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `netem`, each direction | none | 0.1 ms | 0.1 ms, 0.1% loss | 1 ± 0.5 ms, 1% loss | Redis 0.1 ms; clients 25 ± 5 ms, 0.5% loss |
| Round trip to Redis, p50 | 0.3 ms | 5.9 ms | 5.9 ms | 7.1 ms | 5.8 ms |
| Round trip to the server, p50 | 0.4 ms | 5.7 ms | 5.9 ms | 6.1 ms | 57.8 ms |
| Writes, one writer, p50 and p99 | under 1 ms | 9 and 15 ms | 9 and 15 ms | 15 and 232 ms | 62 and 294 ms |
| Writes, 16 writers | 17,422/s, p99 2 ms | 4,973/s, p99 9 ms | 4,454/s, p99 11 ms | 1,177/s, p99 24 ms | 253/s, p99 96 ms |
| Propagation to 5,000 connections, p50 and p99 | 57 and 120 ms | 76 and 127 ms | 79 and 254 ms | 91 and 361 ms | 110 and 348 ms |
| A second replica ready | 3.4 s | 3.6 s | 3.4 s | 6.4 s | 3.5 s |

Through the relays with no delay, the results matched loopback: propagation p99 115 ms against 120 ms.

One data center is 0.1 to 0.5 ms across, between loopback and these 6 ms. One writer, whose writes cross the links alone, met the 20 ms target: p99 15 ms. Propagation p99 was 127 ms, against 120 ms on loopback. 16 writers write less often the farther away they are, as each waits for its answer: that is the load generator, not the server.

Loss costs more than distance. TCP often resends a lost packet only after a timeout, at least 200 ms on Linux. A packet lost on a write's way, from the writer through the server to Redis and back, holds up that write's event for every connection. Of 100 writes measured, one such write sets the p99, and 0.1% loss doubled it, to 254 ms. With 1% lost on every link, one writer's p99 was 232 ms: a write crosses a link four times, in packets of its own, so more than 1% of writes lose one and wait for its resending. Propagation p99 stayed under 500 ms on every network here; the slowest event took 779 ms, with 1% lost.

Over the link to those clients, loading the namespace took 60 seconds instead of 6, and opening the watches 224 seconds instead of 14: the load generator writes 64 at a time and waits 58 ms for each, and all the snapshots of 5,000 clients crossed one relay and one `netem` queue, where real clients would each have a path of their own.

### Leases

100 clients, each with an Instance on its lease (a TTL of 30 seconds, renewed every 10), over a link, for 300 seconds, while a client on loopback watched their Instances:

| The clients' link | Registered in | Fewest Instances seen | Leases expired |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 ± 5 ms each way, 0.5% lost: a round trip of 58 ms | 4.0 s | 100 of 100 | 0 |
| 100 ± 20 ms each way, 5% lost: a round trip of about 200 ms | 17.5 s | 100 of 100 | 3 |

On the second link, a call could wait for several resendings, which is why registering took 17.5 seconds. The three leases that expired held no Instance: the watcher saw all 100 throughout, looking every 100 ms, while an Instance whose lease runs out stays gone until its client finds out at its next renewal, up to 10 seconds later, and registers it again. They fit leases granted to calls whose answer never reached the client, which then asked again: it kept the lease it was given, and the server let the other run out.

### How it was run

The load generator and the server ran in a Linux container on the laptop's Docker VM (OrbStack), on the network of the VM itself, beside Redis and the relays in containers of their own, so that only the VM's kernel stood between them. Through the VM's port forwarding to macOS, packets were lost even without `netem`, and about 5% of the events to 100 connections came 200 ms late, a resending. In this VM, `netem` delays a packet alone on the link by up to a few milliseconds more than told, as the timer that releases it fires late, while under steady traffic packets leave closer to on time: that is why 0.1 ms became a round trip of 6 ms for one request, and why 16 writers saw shorter writes than one. Its jitter also reorders packets, which a real path seldom does. And the same 10 cores ran the server, Redis, the relays and the load generator.

## Not measured

- A real network, or a real data center: the network above was emulated, on one laptop.
- More than one server replica under connection load.
- A Cluster of more than three masters, or more than three replicas.
- Long runs: memory over days, and leaks.

## Reproducing

```bash
COSKY_MEASURE=load COSKY_MEASURE_HEAP=4g ./gradlew :server:test --tests '*LoadMeasurement*'
```

`COSKY_LOAD_CONNECTIONS`, `COSKY_LOAD_WATCHES_PER_CONNECTION`, `COSKY_LOAD_PROPAGATION_PAUSE_MS`, `COSKY_LOAD_RATES`, `COSKY_LOAD_WINDOW` and `COSKY_LOAD_WINDOW_CLIENTS` set the shape. `COSKY_LOAD_SERVER_HEAP` sizes the server, and `COSKY_LOAD_REDIS_URI` uses a Redis you started instead of a container of its own. With `COSKY_LOAD_REDIS_CLUSTER=true` it is a node of a Redis Cluster, whose nodes must announce addresses the run can reach. Many namespaces on several replicas is another test, shaped by `COSKY_LOAD_NAMESPACES`, `COSKY_LOAD_OBJECTS_PER_NAMESPACE`, `COSKY_LOAD_REPLICAS` and `COSKY_LOAD_WRITES`:

```bash
COSKY_MEASURE=load COSKY_MEASURE_HEAP=2g COSKY_LOAD_SERVER_HEAP=2g ./gradlew :server:test --tests '*LoadMeasurement.many namespaces*'
```

`COSKY_LOAD_REDIS_NETEM` and `COSKY_LOAD_CLIENT_NETEM` put a link between the server and Redis, and between the clients and the server, taking the arguments of `tc qdisc ... netem`. Leases over such a link are another test, shaped by `COSKY_LOAD_LEASE_CLIENTS` and `COSKY_LOAD_LEASE_SECONDS`. On a laptop, run them in a Linux container on the Docker host's network, with JDK 21 to build and a Linux JDK 25 for the server, which Gradle finds in `org.gradle.java.installations.paths`:

```bash
docker run --rm --network host -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD":/work -v /path/to/jdk-25:/opt/jdk25 -w /work \
  -e TESTCONTAINERS_HOST_OVERRIDE=localhost -e COSKY_MEASURE=load -e COSKY_MEASURE_HEAP=3g -e COSKY_LOAD_SERVER_HEAP=2g \
  -e COSKY_LOAD_CLIENT_NETEM='delay 25ms 5ms loss 0.5%' eclipse-temurin:21-jdk \
  ./gradlew :server:test --tests '*LoadMeasurement.the targets*' -Porg.gradle.java.installations.paths=/opt/jdk25
```

The failovers come from the scripts in [`testing/failover`](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/main/testing/failover), which start Redis and a server in Docker, on the image of the version in `gradle.properties` unless given another:

```bash
testing/failover/cluster/up.sh && testing/failover/cluster/measure.py 8181 kill && testing/failover/cluster/down.sh
testing/failover/sentinel/up.sh && testing/failover/sentinel/measure.py pause && testing/failover/sentinel/down.sh
```

The hot paths of the client are JMH benchmarks:

```bash
./gradlew :client:jmh
```
</doc>

<doc title="Internals" path="guide/internals.md">
# Internals

For working on CoSky itself. [Architecture](./architecture.md) explains the system, the [design document](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) the reasoning, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` how to send a change.

## Modules

| Module | Holds | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| `api` | Protos, generated code, validation, errors, the OpenAPI document | Nothing |
| `store` | The Store interface, and an implementation in memory | `api` |
| `store-redis` | The Redis Store: the only module with Lua | `store` |
| `server` | gRPC, REST, the Watch cache, the reaper, auth, views | `api`, `store`, `store-redis` |
| `client` | Connections, Watch, leases, snapshots, load balancing. No Spring and no Redis. | `api` |
| `spring-boot-starter` | ConfigData loading, refresh, discovery, registry | `client` |
| `conformance-test` | The suites the Store and the protocol must pass | `store`, `client` |
| `migration` | `cosky-migrate`. The only module that knows 6.x. | `api` |
| `examples` | A provider and a consumer, and the test that runs them | The starter |
| `dashboard` | The React frontend, with a build of its own | The REST API |
| `wiki` | This site | |

The modules that support the build and the tests sit in folders of their own, under the same Gradle paths: `platform/` holds `bom` and `dependencies`, and `testing/` holds `test`, `conformance-test` and `code-coverage-report`.

Two rules hold this together. Nothing but the server touches the Store, and clients never see Redis. And both protocols are one contract: REST is mapped from the same protos as gRPC.

## Building

```bash
./gradlew build
```

Building needs JDK 21, and the server's tests and `:server:run` need JDK 25, and Docker for the tests. Install both JDKs: Gradle does not download them. `./gradlew :server:run --args='--dev'` starts a server in memory.

The server bundles the Dashboard when `dashboard/dist` exists:

```bash
pnpm --dir dashboard install && pnpm --dir dashboard build
```

## Testing

| Level | Where | Against |
|---|---|---|
| Store conformance | `conformance-test`, run by `store` and `store-redis` | Memory, Redis, Redis Cluster |
| Protocol conformance | `conformance-test`, run by `server` | The real services over gRPC |
| Parity of the protocols | `ProtocolParityTest` | The same request over gRPC and REST ends the same way |
| Faults | `FaultInjectionTest` | A real server behind Toxiproxy: partitions, slow links, a hung store |
| Failover | `RedisStoreFailoverTest` | A real Redis losing writes |
| End to end | `examples/e2e` | The server, a provider and a consumer as separate processes |
| TLS | `TlsEndToEndTest` | Both ports, with a generated certificate |
| Dashboard | `dashboard/tests/ui` | A mock answering as the server does |
| Dashboard against the image | `dashboard/tests/ui/real-backend.spec.ts` | The page the image hosts, on that image |
| Migration | `migration` | A real Redis and a real server |

Line coverage has a floor of 90%, enforced by `./gradlew build`. New behaviour should fail a test when you take it out, so try that.

Every pull request also runs Redis 7.0 and Valkey 8, CodeQL, and an image build that starts the image and drives it.

## Lua

All of it is in `store-redis`. Each script keeps to one namespace's hash tag, and declares its keys. The layout is in the design's section on keys.

## Conventions

- Coroutines, carried by virtual threads. Reactor stays in the adapters, which Detekt enforces.
- Errors carry a stable reason, mapped to a gRPC code and an HTTP status in one place.
- A change to behaviour updates the design, and a decision gets a D-number in its table.
- Tests assert behaviour through public interfaces, against real dependencies where it matters.
</doc>
